Background in Low Gravity Smoke The salient result on smoke particle size determination in low-gravity reported by Urban et al.9 is that particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment9 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger tha

n 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft. F. Spacecraft Atmosphere Dust Background Any effort to detect fires must be able to discriminate against the ambient background and nuisance signals. In the case of smoke detection, the background dust aerosol conditions must be considered. The only spacecraft background aerosol particulate measurements to date were made on the Orbiter on STS 32 in 199010 and on the ISS.9 The STS measurements included the results from two cascade impactors and a light scattering device. The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 2.5

to10 μm and >100 μm ranges. The other two ranges < 2.5 μm and 10 to 100 μm were very lightly populated. Each impactor sampled approximately 15 m3 of air over approximately 30 hours. These results showed substantially higher concentrations than typical indoor measurements (over a factor of 5 for the two most populated size ranges). These data were supported by the light scattering instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 locations, all of these reported mass concentrations ranging from 50 to 70 μg/m3. The ISS results of Urban et al.9 were a secondary result of an experiment to validate the operation of an aerosol particle counter in low-gravity. The measurements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cc). The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the STS and the low overall numbers fo

r the ISS suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection since typical normal gravity fires produce substantial particulate in this size range.2,11 However more complete particle size statistics are needed.

II. SAME Experiment Although the CSD experiment produced useful information concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, the data set was not particularly large as the size statistics were obtained from TEM data and critical details were not obtained for the liquid droplet aerosols. To rectify this concern, another experiment (Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment: SAME) was developed. The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and may require substantial sample return to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to mea

sure separate moments of the size distribution. When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled. IV. Conclusion Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity was found to be typically 50% large in count mean diameter than similar conditions in normal gravity. The resultant sizes were all below 300 nm suggesting that discriminating smoke from spacecraft dust possibly could be achieved by detecting in the sub-micrometer range. Numerical modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location and the presence of obstructions.

Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) 30 Day Report Principal Investigator: David Urban, NASA Glenn Research Center Co-Investigators: George Mulholland, University of Maryland Zeng-guang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research Jiann Yang, National Institute for Standards and Technology Thomas Cleary, National Institute for Standards and Technology 1

Final Research Report Template and Guidelines I. Introduction A. Abstract In the wake of the Columbia disaster, NASA Headquarters put out a call for small, low upmass experiments that could be launched aboard the Russian Progress vehicle and which could be made available for launch within a six month period from the date of the request (March, 2003). The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME, formerly known as “Smoke”), which was being developed at the time and which is designed for operation aboard the ISS, required the utilization of a commercially available particulate counter, the TSI P-Trak, that is designed to use gravity to facilitate its operation. The microgravity performance of this instrument was in question and added significant technical risk to the future success of SAME. The Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was designed as a risk mitigation experim

B. Hypothesis Two potential failure modes were identified for the device: 1) that the particulate counting system, containing a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or become obscured and 2) that the internal flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device would cause an over counting of the particulates and give unreliable (high) readings. Therefore, an experiment was designed that would use a functionally flight like design and test it against an aerosol standard and another device (the TSI DustTrak), that was analyzed to be unaffected by the lack of gravity. The choice of the aerosol and the method used to create it were key items. Ideally, a mono dispersed aerosol would be used (0.7 – 1.3 microns), which would allow an easy comparison of the readings from the devices. However, due to the lack of development time, it was proposed to use Arizona Road Dust (ARD, Fine)

instead, in combination with ISS GN2 to create an aerosol for measurement purposes. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses in DAFT: 1) that the TSI P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity, and 2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices C. Objectives of Investigation The objective of DAFT was to minimize the risks of its parent experiment, SAME, by demonstrating that the modified TSI P-Trak functioned effectively and predictably in a microgravity environment.

II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol In order to prepare the P-Trak for operation in microgravity, an analysis of its operation was performed. The P-Trak uses a small pump to draw the sample aerosol through a chamber saturated 2

with alcohol vapor by means of a wick. That vapor/aerosol mix then passes through a cooling tube that allows the alcohol to condense on the particles in the aerosol, making droplets that are large enough to count with a focused laser/photo cell combination. The condenser in the COTS device slopes down, enabling the alcohol from the droplets that adhere to the tube wall to be recycled back to the evaporator. In conjunction with fluid physics researchers at GRC, a modification to the cooling tube was developed that effectively moves liquid alcohol from the tip of the tube back upstream to the evaporator due to capillary action. This was the major modification that was made to the device. Other alterations to the device involved the removal of the mercury switch (for gravitationally sensitive tilt sensor), flight hardening and covering with foil tape for flammability concerns. The TSI DustT

rak, a laser scattering device based on Mie scattering and included as a measurement standard, was hardened in a similar fashion, but did not include a mercury switch. After some consideration, it was decided to use a 15 liter Mylar bag for the containment of the aerosol. Issues, including safety and the atomizing of the particulates (and the fluid that contained them) precluded the use of commercially available mono-dispersed particles. Therefore, Arizona Road Dust (fine), a NIST standard, was selected due to its known constitution and ease of dispersion into a pressurized gas stream. A flight design was created, the parameters tested and determined, and flight like hardware was created and tested with the measurement instruments to develop the correlation curves discussed in the results section. One problem exists with this sample material, however. It contains a given number of partic

les in sizes above 2.5 microns, which is above the measurement limit of the P-Trak. To mitigate this factor, a device, the DAFT Impactor was developed based on design criteria supplied by one of the experiment’s Co-I’s (George Mulholland). The DAFT Impactor is a particle filter for large particles (only) that was designed specifically for the combined flow rate of the test devices. The P-Trak gives a number count of the particles in an aerosol, in readings of pt/cc. Dustrak gives measurements of the total mass, in mg/m3. Since the distribution of the particulates in the aerosol is known to a certain confidence level, and the units had been correlated in testing on the ground, the experiment was conceived to disburse a similar aerosol on orbit and determine the device correlation in a microgravity environment to quantify the P-Trak’s measurement effectiveness. D. Sessions Table D.1 DAFT 1 & 2, Session 1, GMT 54, 2005 The first test point for DAFT was performed on February 22, 2005 during Increment 10. The hardware was set up per the procedure (nominal) in front of EXPRESS Rack 4. Leroy Chiao inserted the batteries to each device, activated them, and performed the zero check. No anomalies were noted 4

(i.e.; warnings, beeping, unreasonable readings, blocked tubing, etc.). The P-Trak was operated for approximately 12 minutes, and continued taking readings for the entire time. Near Real Time (NRT) video was available for most of the test, including set up, and the run time could be approximately synchronized with GMT through its use. The Payload Operations Director (POD) allowed the call up of a request, and Leroy was asked to relay readings from the P-Trak verbally, which he did. Those readings were low (2 – 5 pt/cc). The data for that test point can be seen in Section III C. Figures 1 and 2. A review of that data shows that the readings on both devices were very low for the entire test time, but that upon initial startup, the addition and removal of the HEPA filter (zero check) is clearly indicated in the P-Trak data, and there appears to be some residual dust in the sampling tube tha

t is drawn out during the test point. For the remainder of the point, some small variations can be seen, the DustTrak especially gave low readings. Overall, these readings are almost an order of magnitude below those that would normally be seen in a typical laboratory environment ( ~ 4,000 – 6,000 pt/cc for P-Trak), but were not totally unexpected, due to the presence of a HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system.

D.3 DAFT-3, Session 1, GMT 229, 2006 The first test point for DAFT-3 and -4 was scheduled to be performed on August 18, 2006 (GMT 229), during Increment 13. DAFT required NRT Video. During the hardware was set up procedure in front of EXPRESS Rack 5, Jeff Williams was in the process of unpacking the experiment equipment, and held each item in front of the camera as he unpacked it. When he held up the DAFT Fill Assembly, the ground team noticed immediately that the HEPA filter that supports the pressure relief valves that protect the Sample Bag from being over filled, was missing. The POD was notified and requested to ask Jeff to return the Fill Assembly into the field of view, which he did, confirming the observation. Jeff noted that the HEPA Filter Subassembly was still within the foam enclosure. He then held up that enclosure, and noted that it was permanently deformed. The DAFT Fill A

ssembly is a series of linear tubing connections with ‘appendages’ connected to it by tees. The foam that encased it (minicell) is approximately three times longer than it is wide, and it is about 2 inches thick. From the video, it was clear that the foam was deformed from flat by about one inch along the shorter axis, in line with the thickness. The foam is a ‘donut’ like cutout, with no strength in the direction of the deformation.

At that point, the nominal test plan was aborted. Jeff was asked to restow the Fill Assembly, and to revert to the procedure that was used for DAFT-1 &-2, taking a cabin air sample, which he did. Later, when he attempted to download the data from the devices, another anomaly occurred. When he had attached the P-Trak and attempted the data transfer, the message: “Error Communicating” popped up. The transfer was attempted one more time with the P-Trak and also once with the DustTrak. Backing up in the procedure and attempting to select a com port revealed that the EXPRESS Laptop being used did not have a “Com Port 1” within its list of available choices, which was a problem, since the DAFT Software was configured to use that port.

D.4 DAFT-3, GMT 230, 2006 As a result of the discovery of the broken part on the previous day, a special Safety telecom was convened to determine if the experiment could be performed, and if so, what level of repair or modification would be required to provide the necessary protection for the crew. That telecom involved members of the PSRP, the ISS Cadre, DAFT Project Management and Safety, POIC Safety, the Crew Office and MER Safety. The DAFT engineering team provided several options for repair. They are briefly described as follows: Option 1: Cover the opening to the tubing system with a finger tip, or alternately, with gray tape, and perform the experiment nominally. Option 2: Remove the fitting that supports the Gage subassembly, remove the high pressure relief valve from that subassembly and replace it in that location; and use the remaining fitting to reinstall the low pressure rel

ief valves, without the HEPA filter. Option 3: Disassemble the DAFT Impactor and remove the HEPA filter. Use that HEPA filter to replace the broken one on the Fill Assembly and scavenge the parts from the Impactor that are necessary to deliver the sample to the devices. After a significant discussion regarding the implications and ramifications of each potential fix, it was determined that Option 1, using gray tape to cover the opening, would be the most desirable and did not pose an undue Safety risk to the crew. The engineering team worked with the designated Crew Procedures Engineer (Wayne Wright) to develop the procedures to support that activity, and it was approved for use. Also, the issue regarding the labeling of the com ports on the ELC was worked with the EXPRESS Software group. This issue was resolved when the EXPRESS group renamed the ports to be in compliance with the needs
of the DAFT software. An ISS Payload Anomaly Report (PSR) number (DAFT-HW-01) was issued to describe, record and document the resolution of the broken DAFT Fill Assembly.

List of Pre-, In-, Postflight Anomalies Detailed in the Sessions section. B. Completeness/Quality of Data 7

The data taken from DAFT 1 and 2 can be seen in Section III C. Figures 1 through 4. Test point #2 data (Figures 3 and 4) shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark (P-Trak has a maximum count of 500,000 pt/cc). Although there is no way to exactly correlate between the Velcro demates and the increases in the P-Trak readings, the observations that the unit’s readings increased and decreased in a logical fashion, were within the unit’s prescribed range and there were no observed anomalies serve to indicate that the unit was functioning normally. DustTrak also responded well to the Velcro dust, but did not reach readings above 10% of its overall capability. Test points #3 and #4 were not appreciably different from Test point #1 for either device. Section III C. Figure 7 contains a chart developed from the ground testing th

at was performed in May of 2003, using the crew training hardware in a flight like manner. It can be seen from that graph that although there is a wide variation in the amount of aerosol that is contained within the various samples, the relationship between the DustTrak and P-Trak readings is very linear, meaning that the overall composition of the various aerosols created on the ground, regardless of concentration, is very similar with regard to the relationship between the number and the sizes of the particles entrained. A comparison between this chart and the one taken from the flight data, presented in Appendix C, shows that the data acquired on orbit falls outside of this ground based relationship. The data points are clustered to the left of the line (area), in a region where the count/mass ratio is lower than what was determined from ground testing. This indicates then, that the m

ass of the average particle counted on orbit is higher than that determined on Earth. This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained. It should be noted that, although the DAFT Impactor is designed to filter out the larger particles, it is only about 50% efficient; which implies that it is allowing a considerable number of larger particles to be drawn into the devices. If the data collected on orbit had been to the lower right of the ground based testing line on the graph in Appendix D, it would have meant that more smaller particles would have been present; which is counter intuitive and would have indicated that the P-Trak may have been over counting the particles, one of the postulated failure modes. The analysis of the average particulate size and mass shown on the spreadsheet

in Figure 5 (provided by Zengguang Yuan) shows a good uniformity between the particulates sampled from the various bags. The average mass (assuming a material density of water) is 2.5 E-12 grams, with a range from 2 – 3 E-12. The calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron. The sample material, Arizona Road Dust (Fine) is a standardized, homogenous material; but since it contains a wide distribution of sizes, it is a mixture. The amount of the material that is enclosed in each Dust Holder is small (0.25 gram). From ground testing, it is estimated that only about 10% of the material contained within the Dust Holder is introduced into the aerosol, due to the irregular interior surfaces within it, the surface adhesion of the dust and other factors. H. Conclusion Ideally, DAFT would have collected electronic data from all of the planned 15 test points to establish a large body of consistent, repeated data. Several factors contributed to the decision to not pursue additional test points. They were: Crew Time: Although DAFT was planned for Increment 13, there was not enough crew time available to support all of the desired Payload activities and the prospects for actually performing the experiment at all were extremely uncertain. Fortunately for DAFT, ALTEA had some problems with their hardware and a small block of time came open. DAFT had to negotiate very hard to be allowed the opportunity to schedule 1 + 3 test points, and there was very little chance for another session. Isopropyl Alcohol: As mentioned in the Results section, Jeff Williams was unable to open the DAFT Alcohol Wick container -02. This limited the amount of alcohol a

vailable to support the operation of the P-Trak. Leroy Chiao used this alcohol wick when he performed DAFT-1 and -2 and both of those units were loaded with alcohol over 3 years ago, so the amount that is remaining is highly questionable. Sample Build Up: Testing in the lab has shown that under some circumstances, especially when a significant amount of the larger ARD particles is sent to the devices, a buildup of particles can occur within the optics chamber of the P-Trak. Clearly, the data shows that the sample aerosol contained a greater proportion of larger particles than is experienced on Earth. It also shows that as the run time on the P-Trak is increasing, especially during Bag #3, the count/mass ratio is declining. Although it is not certain that this build up is occurring, the symptoms of that condition are consistent with the data. The lack of the electronic data collection has

limited the ability of the project team to perform a more detailed analysis of the data, since it will remain unknown as to the actual range of the readings over time. The team feels that the information gathered and transmitted by Jeff does represent a good average, but details regarding the data spread could well be lost and not retrievable, since the log functions on both machines seem to have failed (although the possibility of operator error does remain). Based on the limited availability of the crew, it does not seem reasonable to think that time and procedures could be made available for Jeff or the follow on Increment 14 crew to troubleshoot the devices. That being said, DAFT was conceived and built as a Risk Mitigation experiment, not necessarily a Science experiment. It was delivered only 6 months after being proposed and accepted, and it was understood that in some respects,

the sample material (the ARD, a poly disperse particulate) was less than ideal. (Note: For those unfamiliar with the experiment, ideally, a mono disperse aerosol with particulates about 0.7 microns in size would have been created in a density of about 50,000 pt/cc in order to provide a more quantifiable relationship between the readings from the DustTrak and P-Trak. Unfortunately, an aerosol of this type is difficult to manufacture, and the project did not have time or resources to attempt such a development.) The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with no apparent failure. One of the major concerns was that the P-Trak would accumulate alcohol in the optics chamber and obscure them, causing the unit to either read ‘0’ or display and error code. This did not happen. The units gave readings from zero well up into the middle of th

eir operational ranges, and then back; in short, they performed as expected. DAFT-1 and -2 showed that the units were ‘apparently working’ and that the air aboard the ISS is almost unbelievably clean. The readings from the devices during that part of the overall experiment though, never crossed the 20% of the operational range threshold, leaving the results somewhat suspect. 13

This latest experimental run, however, did. The project team feels that the optimal reading range for the P-Trak is from 30,000 – 100,000 pt/cc (although the published range goes up to 500,000 pt/cc) and for the DustTrak; 20 – 80 mg/m3. Clearly, the latest data was within this range. The count/mass ratio between the devices as measured on orbit, although well outside of the value determined on Earth, is both explainable and credible; and to the best of the team’s ability to analyze the data, seems very consistent. The problems with the equipment and the data have been discussed at some length, and although they do leave something to be desired, it does appear that there is enough consistency to determine that the readings recorded are believable and representative of the aerosol created, implying that the units both functioned nominally. Due to the constraints listed above, DAFT-4, using

the ‘unmodified’ P-Trak, was not performed. Since the flight hardware for SAME has been manufactured to the same specifications as the unit that was tested (P-Trak-01), this is not considered to be a factor. The Science team has examined the data and compared the results against the empirical data accumulated for polydisperse aerosols; and determined that the results do have a good basis for acceptance within the bounds of that analysis. For these reasons, the SAME (DAFT) project team feels that the DAFT experiment has been a complete success, and that it has confidence that the P-Traks as designed and manufactured for SAME will perform as accurately and effectively on-orbit as they have in the labs. Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Abstract The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station. Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, burn

er diameter, and co-flow velocity. Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and alth

ough residence time helps explain many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames. Acknowledgments The authors acknowledge G.M. INTRODUCTION SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it was conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered more than a decade time span. During these years, the project experienced a few cycles of active and inactive status. A brief project history is given below. SPICE project was awarded on December 3, 1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Division of NASA Headquarters to Professor Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The original proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment which was a combustion project under NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding letter, the experiment was planned

to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to the end of 1999 was the first phase of the project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabricated and assembled in GRC. Various project reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed. In addition, significant efforts on science side were made to explore proper camera settings for different flame conditions by conducting reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to March 2002, the project was inactive. The second phase of the project was from March 2002 to January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1 Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was switched from

Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware for use with MSG in International Space Station (ISS), which included: designed and assembled Power/Video Unit to support MSG video interfaces, designed and fabricated a new mechanical camera supports, redesigned fuel bottle assemblies and developed new cabling. Project was cancelled again at the end of 2004. ZIN developed storage plan for hardware which was presented to NASA in December, 2004. The SPICE apparatus was put in storage in January 2005 and all the documents were archived waiting for future flight opportunities. At that time, the LSP project and the re-flight LSP-2 were completed, thus the objectives of SPICE were later changed to a standalone investigation of smoke point of jet diffusion flames with coexistence of air flows. One important event

soon after the SPICE became inactive again was the sudden death of Professor Faeth of the University of Michigan, the PI of the project. It was not until March 2006 that the SPICE was resurrected in May, 2006 as part of the Small Payloads Projects Task under MRDOC that Dr. David Urban, the Co-I of the project, succeeded Professor Faeth as the PI of the project. In addition, Professor Peter Sunderland of University of Maryland, former Ph.D. student of Prof. Faeth was recruited as a Co-I of the project. An updated Science Requirement Document was edited. The test matrix was finalized. Additional tests in camera were conducted. Minor hardware modifications were made and a number of project reviews were conducted. h June of 2009. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S.1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting.2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.3 Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion. 1

The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. R

esults from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.

Figure 1. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-buoyant flames The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames.

The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the 2

flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame length wi

th that fuel flow rate. SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP A. Limited by the space in the MSG, SPICE experiment does not have velocity diagnostic capability to reveal the actual velocity in the presence of flame. SPICE FLIGHT TESTS The actual SPICE tests w

ere conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June 23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to clarify any ambiguities. Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support team in TSC. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%. After t

he tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke points. The smoke point lengths, LSP, (and the flow conditions) were obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather transitioned from bright yellow to black over an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Luminous lengths were measured to the point where the centerline grayscale 13

intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This helped reduce the sensitivity of the measured lengths to camera exposures. Totally 526 flames were ignited and studied, which were much more than originally planned. The reason more flames can be studied was owing to the increasing familiarization for astronauts to the apparatus, so that the flame adjusting time and smoke point realization time became shorter and shorter. This leads to plenty unused fuel for new test points. The entire test matrix and measured flame data are listed in Appendix A. The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than the others, attributed to increased soot volume fractions. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with hi

gh air velocity, large burners, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow perturbations. This increased slightly the uncertainties in smoke points for these conditions. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before all desired conditions could be tested, as the supply was limited to two 150 cc bottles of each fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa. Smoke points were attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct. Table 1. Summary of smoke points observeda Parameter

Some smoke points (particularly for propane and ethylene) were identified by the onset of gradual dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames (particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming and reddening near their tips, except when much longer than their smoke points. For these flames, smoke points were identified by the rapid transition to open-tipped flames. Open-tipped flames are common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded4 and are associated with flame extinguishment along the centerline and soot that escapes in an annular shell. For conditions sufficiently above the smoke points, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flames despite the dark background in the video. 14

DISCUSSION Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the fla

me mentioned here refer to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to ass

ociate smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity8,9 and 1000 K in microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than 17

certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex8-11,17,18,2024 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame re

sidence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved rigorously. However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications resulted from the SPICE project listed in
Appendices B through F. The results showed that although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations.

CLOSING REMARKS Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The major conclusions are as follows: 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 5. Consist

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 1. Overview The Flame Design experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Richard L. Axelbaum of the Washington University of St. Louis’s Dept. of Energy, Environmental & Chemical Engineering. The Co-Investigator (Co-I) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the University of Maryland’s Dept. of Fire Protection Engineering. The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Phillip H. Irace who was a doctoral student at the Washington University of St. Louis throughout the on-orbit operations. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (P

S) for ACME including Flame Design and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for Flame Design were conducted in two rounds of testing which occurred in April-July 2019 and Oct. 2021 to Feb. 2022. The two rounds occurred during Increments 59/60 and 66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and ethylene (C2H4) while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. As

a notable exception, the first day of testing in the second round was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with propane (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. The tests on that day were conducted with the long (near) thermocouple rake to acquire data to calibrate optical measurements of the flame temperature through Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). Meanwhile, the short (far) thermocouple rake was used on all other Flame Design test days. Except for the single propane (C3H8) test day previously mentioned, all ISS tests were conducted with the fuel ethylene (C2H4), the inert nitrogen, and the spherical flame configuration. While other conditions had been identified as desired, NASA’s intent was focused rather comprehensive research.

2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of April 2010. The majority of practical combustion processes involve nonpremixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance penalties and possible extinction. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address 3

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish a stated objective. The method involves exchanging nitrogen (or any inert, including carbon dioxide) from the oxidizer stream to the fuel stream such that the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, can be varied with or without affecting adiabatic flame temperature, Tad. The structure of a high Zst flame is substantially different from that of the standard hydrocarbon/air flame, where Zst is relatively low. By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have bee

ther this phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame. This issue can be addressed by performing microgravity experiments because the unique character of nonbuoyant microgravity flames allows the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel into an oxidizer in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer into fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, the long residence times that can be obtained in the spherical flame geometry will allow for validation of a theory that predicts the sooting limits at the limit of infinite Damköhler number, Da. Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a u

nique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction. These findings also suggest that by employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures. The optimum minimum temperature at extinction has led us to propose the concept of a pseudoflammability limit for nonpremixed flames. Again, this fundamental information is most unambiguously demonstrated in quasi-steady, microgravity flames wherein the effects of flame structure can be systematically studied. The proposed work will also allow, for the first time, a strain-free experimental study of the effects of Zst on soot inception and flame extinction processes. Microgravity experiments will involve gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on porous spherical burners and coflow burners.1 Soot incepti
on limits and flame extinction limits will be obtained as functions of Zst, amount of inert, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and computational modeling

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 will support the experimental investigation. Models will include gas-phase and burner-surface radiation. Specifically, soot-inception limits in spherical flames will be measured by establishing a flame at a given Zst and allowing peak temperature to decrease with time until the yellow luminosity is eliminated. The effect of flow direction across the flame will be studied by performing coflow experiments (desired) where the fuel issues into the oxidizer and oxidizer issues into fuel. Gas temperatures will be measured by thin film pyrometry and thermocouples to identify the sootinception temperature. In addition, soot volume fraction measurements will be made to evaluate the effects of Zst and flow direction on soot formation and growth, and to better understand the phenomena of permanently-blue flames. Flame extinction limits will also be

studied in a manner similar to that of soot inception limits, and temperatures near extinction will be measured. The experiments and modeling will yield unique data that will allow for an understanding of how Zst affects soot-inception and flame extinction and how Zst can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction will also be studied and the importance of flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames will be assessed. Finally, the proposed concept of a pseudo-flammability limit for nonpremixed flames will be evaluated and these limits will be ascertained for the test fuels. These results will be useful for the development of future combustion devices that will take advantage of oxygen enrichment technology to design more stable and less polluting flames. __________________________ 1 The coflow flame experiments are desired. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD from April 2010. References and the appendices are not included in this document but can be found in the SRD. The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the value of the spherical, burner-supported nonpremixed flames for flame studies. The one-dimensional flame offers a simple, fundamental configuration to improve our understanding of nonpremixed flame behavior and to explore such effects as radiation and thermophoresis, which are more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al., 1992, Law et al., 2001). The burner-supported spherical flame is in some respects similar to droplet burning but it holds the advantages that larger flames are possible and, with sufficient

ly long time, can approach quasi-steady state. Furthermore, the proposed microgravity coflow flames allow the direction of convection across the flame to be varied. Although the spherically-symmetric flame geometry has many advantages, it is not practical to produce such a flame at normal gravity. The reason for this can be understood by considering the Richardson number, Ri, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force and is given by 5

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) . (2.1) Here g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u burner surface, and ΔΤ = (Tad – Tb), we find that Ri is on the order of 1000 in normal gravity. In fact, it is much higher than this because the more appropriate length and velocity scales are the flame diameter and the velocity at the flame, respectively. The value of Ri can be reduced by judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity. However, Ri for these flames is still on the order of unity, implying that while the flames appear spherical, natural convection is still present. Furthermore, hydrogen must be used as a fuel and be supplied in the ambient so such flames are not relevant to this study. A reduction in Ri can be ac

hieved by reducing the flame size, but substantial reduction in L is not practical because our goal is to produce a flame that is sufficiently large that its structure can be characterized. Furthermore, heat loss to the burner would be excessive for small flames. Consequently, for general fuels and inerts the only practical method of obtaining Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This can be accomplished in a number of microgravity environments, including ground-based facilities, e.g., drop towers for short times, as well as flight experiments, e.g., the International Space Station for longer times. A quantitative evaluation of the acceptable g levels for these experiments is given in Appendix A and is discussed below. The drop-tower results detailed in Section 1.3 have demonstrated the value of the sphericallysymmetric burner stabilized flame. The ability to reverse flow

direction has helped to elucidate the dominant mechanism responsible for permanently-blue flames, yet the results are not conclusive because transient effects could dominate these observations. Transient effects arise from two sources: the ignition process and the long times required for spherical microgravity flames to reach quasi-steady state. The ignition process is not spherically symmetric and thus there is an asymmetry imposed by ignition that must be damped out. More importantly, soot particles that are created during ignition can be trapped in the interior of the flame due to thermophoresis. The particles are trapped for the same reasons that a soot shell is produced in microgravity droplet combustion (Choi et al., 1991, Avedisian and Callahan, 2000). Thus, it is possible for soot to exist in flames after the ignition event even though the flame has ceased producing soot. The rea

son the spherically-symmetric burner-stabilized flame takes so long to reach quasi-steady state is that the radial velocity scales with 1/r2. Thus, at only a few burner diameters away from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant mechanism of transport. Since the characteristic diffusion time τd is given by r2/D, τd is on the order of tens of seconds a few centimeters from the burner. Decreasing the flame size will decrease the size of the thermal field and, consequently, the time to reach quasi-steady state, but there are limits to the minimum flame size that is possible. These limits are imposed by the need to avoid heat loss to the burner and ensure flame sphericity. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility indicate that for many of the run conditions needed for the proposed experiments the flame is still growing significantly after 5 s. Analytical (see Appendix A) and numerical ca

lculations predict that up to 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these run conditions. No ground-based facilities are available to accomplish this. In some ways, the spherical flame experiments are the nonpremixed analog to premixed flame balls because in both systems diffusion dominates the development of the far field temperature distribution. Therefore, this work is subject to the same needs as SOFBALL (Ronney et al., 1998) 6

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 in that long duration microgravity is needed and g-jitter must be negligible because the thermal field is very large and convection is small, i.e., Ri is large even for small g. To provide a quantitative assessment of the acceptable gravity level, an analysis was performed, as detailed in Appendix A. In this analysis, the acceleration induced on a fluid packet by natural convection is formulated by considering a gravitational acceleration given by a sinusoidal function. The resulting acceleration function for the fluid packet is next integrated to obtain the gravity induced flow velocity. This velocity can be converted to an additional mass flux that transports the flame front and causes distortion of the flame. By specifying the maximum percentage of distortion allowed in the experiment (10% here), the acceptable gravity level is determ

ined, and this result is given in Fig. 2.1 for the four flames of Table 1.1. As shown, the required g levels are on the order of 10 μg. This is too for microgravity aircraft, but is consistent with the anticipated environment of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Finally, it is important to emphasize that the proposed experiments illustrate an important and novel use of microgravity for combustion research. In microgravity we are able to hold Zst fixed and in coflow tests vary the direction of convection through the flame. There are no analogous experiments at 1g that can accomplish this. Experiments have been performed in normal gravity coflow flames to understand the effects of flame structure and flow direction on soot formation (Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Skeen et al., 2009). As mentioned previously, owing to the effects of buoyancy on the flow field, the flow direction cannot be
Microgravity gas jet flames in quiescent surroundings have been observed in drop towers and the Space Shuttle and the results have revealed significant differences between the two in terms of 7

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 sooting behavior, suggesting that the drop tower results were far from steady state (Urban et al., 1998). Velocities in coflow flames are similar to those in gas jet flames in quiescent environments. Therefore the impact of buoyancy on coflow flames is expected to have a similar impact to that reported in Urban et al. (1998). Thus, drop tower coflow experiments are not a viable option for studying quasi-steady microgravity coflow flames. The characteristic times in these flames are long and thus the scalar fields develop much slower that in normal gravity, indicating that long duration microgravity is needed.

As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The int

ernal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning.

Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. 10

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C of the ACME Engineering Implementation report. Unfortunately, the spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames, presumably because of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for

Flame Design, Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D of the ACME Engineering Implementation report. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery

B. Hardware Shortcomings From the Flame Design PI, Rich Axelbaum: “The only significant disappointment with the project was with the diagnostics, particularly with respect to gas temperature and soot volume fraction. They were not at the level that the team would have hoped. Much of this was due to the fact that the diagnostics were outdated by the time they were used in our experiments on the ISS, and thus the diagnostics and calibrations were not at the level that we expect in a laboratory experiment. Of course, the ISS has constraints that limit the ability to incorporate stateof-the-art diagnostics, and this likely made this weakness unavoidable, but it would have been valuable to have had more flexibility in terms of being able to upgrade the diagnostics with more modern cameras and instrumentation.” ACME’s sintered spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames

which are centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical symmetry. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center became increasing offset from the burner center as the flow rate was increased. It is very likely that the sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube is more porous than the sintered sphere 18

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supply tube. There was significant improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was replaced mid-way through round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003), which continued to be used for spherical flame testing throughout the remainder of ACME operations. Nonetheless, the symmetry was not perfect, which is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data. On 27 Dec. 2021 (GMT 361), it was determined that the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array was not aligned to the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) as intended, i.e., so that the fibers would be orthogonal relative to the camera. Unfortunately, this was the fourth day of testing in which the fiber array wasn’t aligned, where it regrettably wasn’t recognized earlier. Given the importance of the TFP-derived measurements of

the flame temperature, testing was halted until the array was aligned (with other crew tasks) by astronaut Raja Chari on 17 Jan. 2022 (GMT 017). The signal from the standard ACME radiometer array used in round 1 of Flame Design testing was saturated for nearly every test, yielding non-useful data. For round 2, that sensor array was replaced with the one designed for Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) which yielded satisfactory measurements. ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer did not always perform adequately, where the flow rates were not always appropriately steady or at the intended value. However, the resulting effects on the flame behavior are tentatively assumed to be minor. 4. Preliminary Results A. Changed Test Plans A change was made to the CIR combustion chamber’s pressure limit on 17 Jan. 2022 (by astronaut Raja Chari) to enable Flame Design testing at chamber pressures of up to 3 atm in the final round2 test days, whereas the limit had been 1.5 atm in preceding testing. In his request for this change, Flame Design PI Rich Axelbaum explained: “One of the fundamental goals of Flame Design is to achieve sooting limits. We are unsure if we will be able to attain a range of sooting flames with the current ambient fuel constraints. One way to increase soot formation, and thus the range of the test matrix, is via higher pressures, so this capability can help to ensure we meet our science goals. Another fundamental goal of Flame Design is to understand flame extinction. Our recent analysis suggests that pressure is a critical variable when predicting flame ext

inction, and in can influence flame chemistry in ways that we had not anticipated. Obtaining extinction data over a wide range of pressures could also be valuable for spacecraft fire safety.” An additional normal-flames test day was added to the start of the second round of testing (even though that was focused on inverse flames) to acquire data useful for calibrating the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. With that goal, the added test day, conducted on 28 Oct. 2021 19

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 (GMT 301), was carried out with the long (near) thermocouple rake, where all other Flame Design tests were conducted with the short (far) rake. In his request for this additional test day, the PI stated in part: “The ability to validate the TFP is very important for most of the ACME experiments. Thus, measuring the near-field temperatures under conditions where we have TFP data would be highly desirable, almost required. … These results would be the only measurements ACME has with a direct comparison with TFP, and since we already know exactly which flames to run to get good data, we know that we will be successful in obtaining this data and validating the TFP data. … Reiterating, this extra day would directly benefit all of the temperature data of Flame Design, and all of the spherical flame ACME experiments, by providing at least one d

irect validation of the TFP method. As you know, we have uncertainties about the accuracy of the TFP technique we are using in the ACME rig, and having these T/C measurements could have a profound impact on the ACME results.” As discussed in the previous section, the decision was made to use the CFI-G radiometer array in Flame Design’s second round of testing rather than the standard ACME array that often saturated in the earlier testing. Coiled igniter tips were also used in the second round of testing instead of the loop igniter tips used in the first round, where the coiled were believed to be more robust. As a correction, including two maintenance activities, there were 11 crew days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to prepare for the initial CLD Flame testing on the space station. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these thr

ee consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four

carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the UC I

rvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings. It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Provisions were made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center. All ACME flame tests, including those for Flame Design, were conducted in a nominally automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low rate results f

rom several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz nonimaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for 21

The review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data

Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, recirculation during Flame Design inverse-flame test operations was only conducted prior to venting at the end of a test day. During normal-flame testing, it was usually conducted once in the midst of testing, as done with E-FIELD Flames. Exceptions were test days 19115, 19123, and 19137 (the first three days with flames); 19161 (when no flames were ignited); 19206 (the last test day in the first round of testing), and 21301 (the first day of the second round of testing). Another exce

A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing.
