Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar (2023): In microgravity combustion, where buoyancy is not present to accelerate the flow field and strain the flame, radiative extinction is of fundamental importance, and has implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, the critical point for radiative extinction is identified for normal and inverse ethylene spherical diffusion flames via atmospheric pressure experiments conducted aboard the International Space Station, as well as with a transient numerical model. The fuel is ethylene with nitrogen diluent, and the oxidizer is an oxygen/nitrogen mixture. The burner is a porous stainless-steel sphere. All experiments are conducted at constant reactant fl

ow rate. For normal flames, the ambient oxygen mole fraction was varied from 0.2 to 0.38, burner supply fuel mole fraction from 0.13 to 1, total mass flow rate, mtotal , from 0.6 to 12.2 mg/s, and adiabatic flame temperature, Tad , from 2000 to 2800 K. For inverse flames, the ambient fuel mole fraction was varied from 0.08 to 0.12, burner supply oxygen mole fraction from 0.4 to 0.85, mtotal from 2.3 to 11.3 mg/s, and Tad from 2080 to 2590 K. Despite this broad range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2 s for normal flames, and an oxygen- based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. With this information, a simple equation is developed to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactan

t mass flow rate. Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusionlimited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth.) Abstract for On the existence of steady state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames in the presence of radiation heat loss (2023): Whether steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion exist in the presence of radiation heat loss is an important fundamental question and has important implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, experiments aboard the International Space Station and a transient numerical model are used to investigate the existence of steady-state microgravity spherical diffusi

on flames. Gaseous spherical diffusion flames stabilized on a porous spherical burner are employed in normal (i.e., fuel flowing into an ambient oxidizer) and inverse (i.e., oxidizer flowing into an ambient fuel) flame configurations. The fuel is ethylene and the oxidizer oxygen, both diluted with nitrogen. The flow rate of the reactant gas from the burner is held constant. It is found that steadystate gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist in the presence of radiation heat loss, provided that the steady-state flame size is less than the flame size for radiative extinction, and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss does not drop the flame temperature below the critical temperature for radiative extinction (1130 K). A simple model is provided that allows for the identification of initial conditions that can lead to steady-state spherical diffusion flam

es. In the spherical, infinite domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusioncontrolled system to effectively reach steady-state is found to be on the order of 100,000 s. Despite a narrow range of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary. Steadystate flames are simulated using the numerical model for over 100,000 s. 25

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 Abstract for Observations of long duration microgravity spherical diffusion flames aboard the international space station (2021): Spherical diffusion flames of gaseous fuels supported on a porous spherical burner are investigated experimentally in microgravity for long durations aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Experimental results are compared with a transient numerical model. The experiments involve normal spherical diffusion flames (i.e., fuel flowing into oxidizer) burning ethylene in an oxygen/nitrogen mixture at atmospheric pressure. The stoichiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature are varied by diluting the fuel with nitrogen and varying the oxygen concentration in the ambient. The diagnostics consist of color video, thin-filament pyrometry for gas temperature, thermocouple measurements of burner te

mperature, and photomultiplier tube measurements of broad and narrow-band flame emission. Burn times range from 28 –336 s. All flames grow monotonically after ignition. Peak gas temperature generally decreases with time. Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release. Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms. The oscillations grow in magnitude until complete extinction. Sufficiently small flames with low radiation losses exhibit quasi-steady behavior, but burner heating is significant, and the experimental duration is dictated by the temperature limit of the porous sphere. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel

method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.

I. Introduction The Flame Design experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve the understanding of soot inception and control, in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the ‘design’ of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." 31

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 Flame Design investigates the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames created with porous spherical burners. Tests are conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (e.g., ethylene) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. More specifically, Flame Design has the following experimental objectives which are listed here in priority order. It must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired or highly desired testing with carbon dioxide, pressure as a variable (except to a limited degree), coflow flames, or methane. A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for C2H4 and CH4* flames. Identify the corres

ponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames**. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4*. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. Obtain similar measurements for inverse and normal coflow flames**. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 * flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames. Measure blowoff limits for inverse and normal coflow flames**.

*desired; **highly desired The majority of practical combustion processes involve the non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient, and the resulting emissions must be low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance penalties and possible extinction. The Flame Design study considers an innovative method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutan

ts. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame, in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish the desired objective. This method involves shifting the nitrogen from the air (or oxygen/nitrogen mixture) to the fuel stream, such that the mixing that occurs at the flame can be varied with or without affecting the flame temperature. [This can also be done with inerts other than nitrogen and oxygen/inert 32

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 mixtures other than air.] Such nitrogen exchange has enabled the production of the flames that are soot-free at all flow conditions, i.e., which are ‘permanently blue.’ The Flame Design experiment involves gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on a porous spherical burner. Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits are obtained as functions of the nitrogen exchange, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and computational modeling support the experimental investigation, where they are facilitated by the spherical flame shape enabled by the microgravity environment. Models include gas-phase and burner-surface radiation. Buoyant gravity-driven flow complicates the interpretation of the existing results and has led to different theories to explain the permanently-blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether thi

s phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame, or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame. The challenges of normal-gravity studies are avoided by performing the tests on the International Space Station (ISS), where the non-buoyant microgravity flames allow the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel from the burner into an oxidizer (e.g., air) in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer from the burner into an atmosphere of fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) i

nstability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion –

regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. Flame Design should yield unique data that allows for a better understanding of how nitrogen exchange affects soot-inception and flame extinction, and how it can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction are also studied, and the importance of the flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames is assessed.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol Flame Design and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the flow

rate can be adjusted to approach a flame’s soot limit. This was not done during Increments 59 and 60, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

III. Results A. These tests featured normal flames, where gaseous fuel was ejected from a porous spherical burner into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. In contrast, the upcoming second round will feature tests with inverse flames, where the oxidizer is ejected from the burner into a fuel/nitrogen atmosphere. As a result, the second round flames will be ‘inside out.’ It is currently expected that the second round of tests will be conducted during Increment 63. The ‘interruption’ in the Flame Design testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests t

o maximize its scientific outcome. Flame Design does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with the gaseous fuel ethylene (C2H4). It is a simple hydrocarbon gas for which the chemistry is well understood and it is typically highly sooting because of its carbon double bond. The tests were conducted with both pure fuel 34

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 1. Mission anomalies There were no significant anomalies hindering Flame Design operations during Increments 59-60, but there was a pertinent anomaly that had previously occurred. It was discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle for the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle had been on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was replaced on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration. 2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data Flame Design tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software script), where

that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. Such aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU). These are infrequent, but there are sometimes days when ACME tests have aborted repeatedly. ACME tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed. Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically

avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection.

C. Completeness/Quality of Data The number of flames ignited in the round 1 testing significantly exceeds the normalflame tests which were specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD). A total of 41 normal-flame tests were identified as required for the Flame Design experiment. In great contrast, 188 flames of this type were ignited in the experiment, so more than 4.5 times as many flames were ignited than required. However, as discussed in Section III.A, the performance of the first spherical burner was not always satisfactory – where the flame was not always sufficiently spherical or centered on the burner, suggesting extreme asymmetry in the flow field and thus 37

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 questionable data. Yet, 102 flames were ignited with the second burner, which is nearly 2.5 times the number of required normal-flame tests. ACME’s sintered spherical burners do not yield spherically symmetric flames which are centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical symmetry. This lack of symmetry is especially evident at high burner flows. It is very likely that the sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube is more porous than the sintered sphere itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supply tube. There was significant improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was replaced mid-way through round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003). But the symmetry is not perfect and this is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data. Portions of ACME’s

recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. E. Preliminary Research Findings Flame Design results have shown that spherical diffusion flames in microgravity have unique characteristics that are valuable for fundamental studies of diffusion flames. Flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size such that very small flames - just above their kinetic extinction limits - have low radiative loss, and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior. Larger flames increase in size over time until the rate of radiative heat loss exceeds the rate of chemical heat release, and the flame extinguishes via radiative extinction. Before total extinction occurs in these flames, they experience an unstable, oscillatory mode, in which they partially extinguish and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude until total extinction. For constant ambient oxygen conc

entration, larger flames (with higher fuel flow rates) radiatively extinguish faster than smaller flames (with lower flow rates) due to higher radiative losses and decreasing chemical heat release. Small, asymptotically quasi-steady flames are found to have low radiative losses and nearly constant chemical heat release. A thorough analysis of low flow rate flames was completed in order to investigate the existence of steady-state spherical flames, which has been a subject of debate in literature. This analysis is described in the submission to the 38th International Symposium on Combustion cited below. 1. P. Irace, H. Lee, K. Waddell, L. Tan, D. Stocker, D. Urban, P. Sunderland, and R. I. Introduction The Flame Design experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve the understanding of soot inception and control, in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the ‘design’ of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. 42

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design investigates the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames created with porous spherical burners. Tests are conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (e.g., ethylene) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. More specifically, Flame Design has the following experimental objectives which are listed here in priority order. It must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired or highly desired testing with carbon dioxide, pressure as a variable (except to a limited degree), coflow flames, or methane. Measure blowoff limits for inverse and normal coflow flames**. *desired; **highly desired The majority of practical combustion processes involve the non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient, and the resulting emissions must be low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance penalties and possible extinction. The Flame Design study considers an innovative method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes

a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame, in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish the desired objective. This 43

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 method involves shifting the nitrogen from the air (or oxygen/nitrogen mixture) to the fuel stream, such that the mixing that occurs at the flame can be varied with or without affecting the flame temperature. [This can also be done with inerts other than nitrogen and oxygen/inert mixtures other than air.] Such nitrogen exchange has enabled the production of the flames that are soot-free at all flow conditions, i.e., which are ‘permanently blue.’ The Flame Design experiment involves gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on a porous spherical burner. Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits are obtained as functions of the nitrogen exchange, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and computational modeling support the experimental investigation, where they are facilitated by the spherical flame shape enabled b

y the microgravity environment. Models include gas-phase and burner-surface radiation. Buoyant gravity-driven flow complicates the interpretation of the existing results and has led to different theories to explain the permanently-blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether this phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame, or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame. The challenges of normal-gravity studies are avoided by performing the tests on the International Space Station (ISS), where the non-buoyant microgravity flames allow the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel from the burner into an oxidizer (e.g., air) in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer from the burner into an a

tmosphere of fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity

flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. Flame Design should yield unique data that allows for a better understanding of how nitrogen exchange affects soot-inception and flame extinction, and how it can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction are also studied, and the importance of the flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames is assessed. 44

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 II. Methods/Research Operations B. Discussion of Method/Protocol Flame Design and other ACME experiments were configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role was to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes included the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All ACME testing was commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of ACME testing was conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. While it was possible to make some ‘manual’ changes outside of the script, e.g., to approach a flame’s soot limit, during a test that was not done in any ACME testing, neglecting minor exceptions, e.g., to terminate tests afte

r the flames had extinguished. Testing was not conducted when thrusters fired or spacecraft docked or undocked from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data was downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data Flame Design tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. Such aborts normally occured because of communication issues with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU). These were infrequent, but there were some days wh

en ACME tests aborted repeatedly. ACME tests were of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. In the first round of Flame Design testing, the igniter tip failed twice requiring crew time to be scheduled to replace it before the subsequent test day could be conducted. Regrettably, it was sometimes discovered during ACME testing that the igniter had failed during the final test of the preceding test day, where an example was on 10 June 2019 (19161) when no flames were ignited as a result (as discussed in section III.A). An igniter check was subsequently added to the ACME end-of-test-day procedure to avoid such recurrences. However, on another test day, it was believed that the igniter tip had failed but ignition was instead prevented because the chamber pressure exceeded the pressure switch limit. Ignition was achieved after the chamber pressure was appropriately reduced. T

he first test of the day has also sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed. Ignition was also sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection were such that the detection threshold was reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of 48

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 the detection, the hot-wire igniter was deactivated and retracted, which was of course an issue when the flame has yet to ignite. This was typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection.

Week 8: April 26 – May 2 On GMT 115, the first ACME Flame Design test points were performed. Pure gaseous ethylene fuel was ejected into air from a porous sphere, which, in microgravity, results in a one-dimensional, spherical flame. Thus, data analysis is greatly simplified because the flame shape doesn’t need to be predicted, and computational modeling can focus on the detailed chemistry and transport of the molecules and energy. The goal of Flame Design is to improve our understanding of soot processes so that flames can be “designed” to be soot free. This research could help lead to reduced soot and NOx—and thus reduced smog and acid rain—through nitrogen exchange, where the nitrogen is shifted from the air to the fuel. This oxygen-enriched combustion of diluted fuel could also facilitate carbon sequestration (i.e., capture and storage).

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 As can be seen in Figure 1, the flame is nominally spherical, but heat loss to the burner tube causes it to locally quench. Similarly, candle flames have an open gap close to the candle, again due to heat loss. These non-premixed flames are a bit like bubbles, where the flame is the shell where the fuel and oxygen combine and create heat, light, and chemical products like carbon dioxide and water. In premixed flames, the fuel is within the “bubble” and the oxygen is outside of it. Future Flame Design tests are planned where the flame will be inside out, i.e., inverted. To conduct those tests (planned for 2020), the CIR's Combustion Chamber will be filled with a fuel/nitrogen mixture while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture will flow from the burner.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 While Flame Design’s primary objective is to determine the conditions under which flames are soot-free or soot producing, a secondary objective is to establish flammability limits for these spherical flames. We have observed interesting phenomena where the flames sometimes self-extinguish after growing oscillations. These oscillations are apparent in the above graph, which shows the chemiluminescence from excited molecules that drop to a lower energy state by emitting a photon at a specific wavelength. CH* chemiluminescence is the source of most of the blue seen in hydrocarbon flames and OH* chemiluminescence is in the ultraviolet. These two measurements are made with Photomultipiler Tubes (PMTs), where each tube is equipped with a narrow-band filter corresponding to an excited molecule. In the example shown in the graph, the flame’s osc

illations lasted about 30 seconds and occurred at roughly 1 Hz, but they slowed in frequency as they grew in strength. The oscillations are evident in the imaging, where the flame locally quenches—creating a hole in the flame. This hole allows for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which in turn results in a recovery of the flame. The size of the opening in the flame (which normally separates the fuel and oxygen) grows with time until the entire flame extinguishes. Interestingly, the graph shows that the CH* measurement was relatively steady before the start of the oscillations in comparison with the decaying OH* emission. This difference will be further examined to improve our understanding of flame extinction.

CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG This test point video shows a sooty flame, and, in the absence of buoyancy, the soot stays within the flame and clusters. Some of the glowing soot clusters move out of the flame due to the outward flow of the diluted ethylene fuel through the burner’s porous sphere. In contrast, some of the clusters get trapped within the flame due to a temperature gradient that moves them inward toward the cold burner and away from the hot flame. After some time, the harp-like array of 14-micron ceramic fibers is translated into the flame to determine the radial temperature distribution. Using a carefully characterized camera, the temperature can be quantitatively determined from a glowing fiber’s color, where yellow is hotter than orange, and orange is

hotter than red. The motion of the fiber arm causes the soot clusters to move away from the fibers. While the temperature measurements are being made, the flow of diluted ethylene is gradually reduced, which causes the flame to become smaller and unstable. Heat loss causes the flame to locally quench—creating a hole in the flame near the burner tube. This hole allows for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which reinvigorates the flame and causes it to close again. The flame opens and closes, effectively consuming fuel in repeated gulps…a bit like a video-game character eating dots. But as the fuel flow is reduced further, the size of the open “mouth” gets smaller, as if the flame is becoming full. The flame becomes stable again until the flow becomes so small that the flame finally goes out. This video illustrates the extreme complexities of even conceptually simple flames! Even th

ough mankind has been using combustion for millennia, microgravity research can unlock new understanding, which would lead to improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion.

Although the pressure didn't greatly affect the size of the flames, it still had a significant effect. The flame at lower pressure is much brighter because at higher pressures light-emitting molecules are more likely to be extinguished due to molecular collisions. Also, the low-pressure flame shows subtle signs of soot formation. At the top of the flame, the blue edge is tinted with yellow due to soot, which also creates a haze just above the flame. Inverse flames are inside out, where the soot is formed outside of the flame when the hot fuel combines with itself in the absence of oxygen (which is inside the flame). The porous spherical burner is illuminated in red from the illumination package we sometimes use during imaging.

Week 16: Jan. 28 – Feb. 3 On GMT 027, we ignited 16 inverse flames for ACME Flame Design. We performed these tests in a combustion chamber filled with an ethylene/nitrogen mixture to a pressure of 3 atm. We plan to compare these tests to earlier ones performed at lower pressures. During all tests, the 14-micron ceramic fibers were translated into the flame to optically measure the flame temperature through a technique known 70

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). On GMT 031, Pyotr Dubrov replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of Flame Design test points. Figure 1. Temperature Measurement of a Flame Design Inverse Flame In this false-colored image, one 14-micron ceramic fiber was inserted into the flame where a second fiber is visible just above. Both fibers are hot enough to visibly glow, where the temperature can be quantitatively determined from their hue using a camera characterized for that purpose. The flame temperature is determined from where the fiber passes through the flame shell and glows most brightly.

Week 17: Feb. 4-10 On GMT 035, we performed the final test points for the second round of testing for ACME Flame Design. We ignited 15 inverse flames. For these tests, we filled a combustion chamber with ethylene/nitrogen mixtures and then flowed a mixture of oxygen/nitrogen from the burner. Tests were conducted at both elevated and reduced pressures. The spherical symmetry of the flames, resulting from the absence of buoyant flows created by Earth's gravity, simplifies data analysis and can lead to new understanding. These were our final test points with ACME, which has been successfully performing science in CIR since 2017!

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 Figure 1 shows the inverse spherical flame growing with time to reach enough fuel to consume the oxygen flowing from the porous spherical burner. As the flame grew bigger, the radiative heat loss increased, which caused the flame to weaken and become dimmer. The flame's temperature dropped, which is indicated by the hue of the glowing ceramic fibers, where yellow is hotter than orange, which in turn is hotter than red. 72

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection The Flame Design data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where that is generally true for the ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The Flame Design image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used at least generally with a CH* filter 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format as well as a converted Tagged Image File (tif) for

mat. NASA’s post-processing of the raw images was carried out without each of the following: a. color balancing (to avoid possible saturation) b. dark frame subtraction c. removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage) Furthermore, the conversion employed a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) because it will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers. The images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are provided in a tif format. Meanwhile, the analog operations (ops) video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was used during

a limited number of Flame Design test days and the resulting raw data files are in a text (i.e., ASCII) format. Consult the forthcoming ACME/Flame Design Data Interpretation document to learn more. The raw Flame Design data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 1. Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory d

rop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G testing was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with gaseous fue

l (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred during the first round of testing. CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned rather than gaseous fuel. Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight

by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other ACME experiments, primarily from ZIN Technologies, Inc.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a

broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight experiment. The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on coo

l flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. Broader Impacts: The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry. It should advance the state-of-the-a

rt in cool flame kinetics mechanisms, which in turn could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. This project will have several educational impacts. Graduate students will conduct much of the 4

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 research. The research results will be integrated into three combustion courses taught by the PI. The PI will team with two organizations at UMD - the Women in Engineering Program and the Center for Minorities in Science and Engineering - to foster interest in science and engineering among female and minority secondary school students. A day-long flame laboratory will be developed for secondary school students that will foster their interest in combustion and scientific inquiry.

normal gravity. This can be explained by considering the Richardson number, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity environment. Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames

, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX-2, and CFI droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. Analytical work supports these observations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and

numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide this environment. 5

Science Objectives The objectives text presented here is the ‘Hypotheses and Objectives’ section (1.3) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will c

ause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. The research objectives of the proposed work are as follows. 1. Plan and support flight testing on the ISS. 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. References to other sections within the boxed text of this section refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document. ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately describe the final engineering in some regards. Therefore updates, clarifications, additional details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, whic

Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measur

ed to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning. 7

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.

Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (sFlame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitro

gen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premix
ed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 8

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog ca

mera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Lightemitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The nat

ural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted

for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. The clear “filter” is of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Re

port (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras. 9

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second (fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During

set up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements. For an example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers: P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750. B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S-type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the Comb

ustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array. Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest downstream position. Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and for all of the CFI-G testing. CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction. This will be accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the camera and the collimated lig

ht source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at opposite windows. The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps. Thus far, the primary purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for determination of the droplet burning rate. A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much, but not all, of ACME’s operations. In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera is very insensitive to blue. Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing. Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for determinations of soot volume fraction

es deleted without downlinking to enable additional testing. And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value. Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E-FIELD Flames experiment. This was a design trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical instruments. CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier (for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging. Again as a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. During ACME operations, the LLL-UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. While

not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the performance of additional tests. This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was generally configured with its CH* filter, where an exception is some s-Flame testing with particularly dim flames. Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the flame. More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT4600. The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non-imaging optical diagnostics including both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs). There is a crew-exchangeable linear array of radiometers of which there are two vers

ions supporting the initial set of experiments. The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other instrumentation. One array is equipped with a single wide-view radiometer with two narrowview radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4. The narrow-view radiometers are intended to support studies of gas-jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, making the “lower” detectors useful. The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wideview measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission 11

Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the crew, alternate arrays could be developed. Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard (ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner. B. Hardware Shortcomings CFI-G’s two primary challenges were in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non-premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. Meanwhile, evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing. During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion. In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from interve

ning low-temperature combustion. It appears that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons. The catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the lowtemperature combustion in these tests. A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain was set high. There were also issues with the Image Processing and Storage Units (IPSUs) which affected CFI-G operations. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. load Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew 18

Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames: An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model

is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial-burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and formaldehyde emissions. These are the

first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K. Cantera autoignition simulations for homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool flame temperature of 885 K, which is significantly higher than observed. Publications: • M. Impacts, Benefits, and Products Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The meas
urements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH Dr. Vedha Nayagam, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growin

g field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved unders

tanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of t

he fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The additional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. D. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI-G. Furthermore, the CFI-G tests were conducted using the 29

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have

a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application.

II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. No CFI-G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exceptio

n of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 30
