Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combust

ion, nonpremixed cool flames can be directly by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. A challenge for cool flame detection is concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain is set high. When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. Mor

e specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that the lowest of the 14-micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken. Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array. Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 5 mm apa

rt. Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also has months of remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers (instead of 5) for the final BRE testing, the subsequent CLD Flame tests, and at least

Completeness/Quality of Data Only the first 3 of 22 CFI-G test days were conducted during Increment 64, so only a small fraction of the test matrix has been completed. In this regard, CFI-G testing is expected to continue through most of Increment 65. The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). Recorded i

mage data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints.

D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate, atmospheric O2 concentration, fuel dilution, and pressure were obtained. The raw test measurements made from devices - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test. The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec. The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements. The transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis. In addition, test images recorded in tiff and hobj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME DataCam have been analyzed to find flame diameters. Of these the intensified camera is of most value and all of its images to date have been

converted to video files and reviewed. Particular attention has been given to the PMT-2 measurements due to its sensitivity to wavelengths of 230 – 700 nm for CH2O* to investigate the presence of cool flames. PMT-2 measurements have been analyzed to determine flame durations as well.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Burner temperatures will be analyzed to find their correlation to the cool flame diameters. E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. Maryland investigator team] The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified camera images we do not believe any self-sustained cool flames were created. While it is possible that momentary cool flames were created, these are difficult to detect without increasing the gain on the intensified camera before the hot flames extinguish, which is planned. The video record will furnish excellent measurements of flame diameter versus time for a broad range of fuels and conditions. Mission anomalies On Aug. 30 (GMT 242), the primary Image Processing and Storage Unit, used to record the imaging from both the ACME DataCam and CFI intensified camera (IPSU-G, also known as IPSU5), caused issues and eventually stopped working. Only the first two tests on that day were successful, where two tests aborted due to an IPSU error, and three tests failed to ignite. In closing checkout, it was determined that the hot-wire igniter tip had also failed. With the IPSU-G failure, the test day was nearly a total loss. Except for a small number of sample images downloaded during the midst of testing, the primary image data from even the successful tests was lost. Furthermore, there was no more propane available for use in inverse-flame testing, so the test day could not be repeated

. However, astronaut Mark Vande Hei replaced the failed igniter tip on Sept. 8 and the failed hard drive in the IPSU-G on Sept. 10, and CFI-G testing successfully resumed on Sept. 13, just 2 weeks after the double failure. Looking back to Increment 64, the Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU1) used with the High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and the opposed CIR illumination package ceased functioning on March 29 (GMT 088). Tests 21088M1-M3 aborted due to an error with IPSU1 communication, where test M4 was successful when the test was run without use of the HiBMs camera. The troublesome IPSU1 was replaced by astronaut Megan McArthur on May 18 (GMT 138), but it was not available during the intervening test days. However, this wasn’t particularly a loss to CFI-G because that camera, with its red filter, is only sensitive to the red backlight from the CIR illumination package

and visible thermal radiation, e.g., from glowing soot particles. Furthermore, the illumination could make it more difficult to discern cool flames, so the HiBMs camera, illumination package, and IPSU1 were rarely used for CFI-G. The principal exception was during the second round of testing. With the inverse-flame tests, the soot is generated outside of the flames, so this photography was used to track potential soot deposition on the chamber windows, etc. However, the end-of-day imaging did not appear to change over time, suggesting that the soot was not an issue for the chamber windows. However, the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules and radiometers were closer to the flame than the windows and might had been adversely affected by soot. 4. In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening lowtemperature combustion. It is likely that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons. The catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the lowtemperature combustion in these tests. A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain

is set high. When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame

locally quenches near the supply tube. Status of Data Analysis [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate (for normal flames), the oxidizer mass flow rate (for inverse flames), O2 concentration, fuel dilution, and pressure were obtained for all the normal and inverse flame test days. The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec. The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements. The transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis. K. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] A total of 280 hot diffusion flames were observed. Among them, 189 flames experienced radiative extinction, and the rest were extinguished when their flow was terminated, either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated. Of those that extinguished radiatively, 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames. These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% nbutane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s. Cool diffusion flames were initially identified by the readings of radiometers after the radiative extinction of hot flames. Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the

radiative extinction of a hot flame. Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped flowing. Figure 1(c) shows multiple hot-cool flame transitions. The first cool flame, the first drop of the radiant heat flux, followed the radiative extinction of the first hot flame. In a few seconds, the heat flux abruptly increased due to reignition of a hot flame. This cycle of radiative extinction, transition to a cool flame, and reignition of a hot flame continued until the flow was terminated. The observed cool flames are summarized in Table 3. Cool flames were also identified by processed images taken from the intensified camera. When cool flames appeared after the radiative extinction of the hot flames, no flame luminosity was evident for about 1 s, after which cool flames appeared. For test points 21174C3, C4, C6, and F1, the cool flames lasted for app

roximately 14 s and disappeared as soon as the fuel flow stopped. For the tests of multiple hot-cool flame transitions, 21291A1 and 21291C1, the first cool flame lasted longer than the following cool flames. The intensified camera images of hot and cool flames were used to find flame radii as well. The radii of hot flames were measured at the time just before the flame oscillation. Figure 1. Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Oxidizer Flow Rates Figure 1 compares the flames from three tests with different flow rates of oxidizer from the burner. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g., carbon dioxide and water vapor). Flames of hydrocarbon fuels are naturally blue, while the hightemperature soot glows red, orange, yellow, or even white depending on its temperature. At igni

tion, this flame was all bright and sooty, but the system is not fully symmetric. There is some asymmetry to the burner flow, and there is heat loss to the tube supplying the gas to the porous spherical burner. As a result, the soot faded from the lower hemisphere, which in this image appears to be soot free. Meanwhile, the upper hemisphere remained enveloped in a layer of glowing soot. Tests like this have yielded valuable data for improving our understanding of how to control soot generation.

Week 27: Oct. 8-14 On GMT 285, Megan McArthur configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support an extra day of testing for CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Part 1 studies normal flames as opposed to inverse flames like Part 2. For normal flames, the gaseous fuel flows from the burner into a Combustion Chamber filled with diluted oxygen. The reverse is true for inverse flames, making them inside out. The purpose of this extra day is to recreate the test conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing. The goal of CFI-G is to study these low temperature flames to gain valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines. Also, to support this extra day of testing, Shane Kimbrough set the CIR Valve Timers and replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 on GMT 286 and Megan McArthur replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #4 on GMT 287

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Increment 66 Week 1: Oct. 15-21 On GMT 291, we performed the last 12 tests for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) during an extra day of testing with normal flames. The purpose of this extra day was to recreate the test conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing, and we successfully achieved cool flames! In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames. Cool flame chemistry is important for ignition in internal combustion engines and an improved understanding would aid the development of vehicles that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution

While the low-temperature cool flames between the hot flames aren’t visible in this video, they cause the closest thermocouple to warm enough to visibly glow prior to reignition. Reignition causes the temperature to abruptly increase, but then it drops while the hot flame burns and weakens. When the hot flame extinguishes and transitions to a cool flame, the temperature starts increasing again until another temperature spike caused by the next reignition. In another test, we saw evidence of a cool flame where the temperature temporarily rose after the hot flame extinguished but not enough to reignite a hot flame.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 1. Overview The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Chung K. Law of Princeton University. The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), namely Prof. Stephen D. Tse of Rutgers University and Dr. Kurt R. Sacksteder of the NASA Glenn Research Center. While Sacksteder was actively engaged in defining the experiment, he had transitioned to other NASA work long before the spaceflight operations limiting his overall contributions. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for

ACME including s-Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Vedha Nayagam and Uday G. Hegde who are also with CWRU. The s-Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 60-63, where there was no testing during Increment 62 due to limited crew availability. More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Sept. 2019 to Jan. 2020, while the second-round testing – featuring helium rather than nitrogen dilution - occurred from May to July 2020.

2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of Jan. 2010. Recognizing that most combustion engines and devices operate on the basis of diffusion flames, the proposed program aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well-defined flow fields such that the phenomena of interest can be studied without being unduly complicated and compromised by complex and sometimes non-quantifiable flow field effects. The basic flame configuration adopted for the investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing ambience in microgravity. The onedimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulat

ion. The primary goals of the program are two-fold and strongly interdependent. The first objective is to interrogate the fidelity of the chemical kinetic mechanisms and transport submodels used in the simulation of aerothermochemical phenomena, and consequently identify possible modifications. The second objective is to characterize and gain predictive capability on spherical diffusion flames.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the movement of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition from a non-steady-state condition and their extinction boundaries due to direct finite-rate chemistry and indirect radiative heat loss. The emphases are on the relative importance of radiative emission and re-absorption, the examination of the adequacy of the detailed chemical kinetics mechanism and transport submodels used, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. Results of the study are of relevance to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to a non-steady-state initial condition with respect to the aspects given in (1)

. The studies will include characterizing soot onset as a function of residence time for expanding flames, as well as soot radiation and transport contributions in spreading, extinction, and instability. The project involves microgravity experimentation, computational simulation, and, where appropriate, theoretical analysis. Interpretation of all phenomena will emphasize the simultaneous and coupled influence of chemistry and transport.

B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity Environment’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD from Jan. 2010. See the SRD itself for the references, etc. which are not included in this report. 2.5.1 Limitations of Terrestrial (1g laboratory) Testing We seek to make observations of truly one-dimensional flames whose structure can be studied without complications due to uncertainties in the flow pattern caused by buoyancy. Such fundamental study of flame structure and dynamics is best served via the elimination of buoyancy through the reduction of gravity. The minimum sizes of these flames imply that buoyancy would be significant if the experiments were conducted in normal gravity. Previous experimentation on earth has amply demonstrated this influence. Although studies of spherical diffusion flames were conducted in normal gravity using the

low-pressure, inverse-flame arrangement (see §1), the conditions are limited for small flames, low pressures, low molecular weight fuels. Indeed, only the hydrogen flame can be considered to be nearly buoyancy free. With such constraints, normal-pressure, micro-gravity, hydrocarbon-based experiments are requisite. One-dimensional spherical flames allow for the unambiguous study of such fundamental flame phenomena as the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames (including the mechanisms of flame front unsteadiness), soot suppression/formation, and flame front instabilities, without gravity-induced baroclinicity and buoyancy, on the flame responses.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 2.5.2 Limitations of Drop Towers and Aircraft Extensive experimentation has been conducted in the 2.2-s drop tower, 5-s drop tower, and parabolic aircraft, as reviewed previously in §1.3. Although experimental data of good quality were obtained on the transient response of spherical diffusion flames in the 2.2-s drop tower facility, the duration was insufficient to observe radiative extinction. The numerical simulations indicate that, for the characteristic flames under study, more than 2.5s of microgravity time is needed. Subsequent parabolic aircraft experimentation afforded the additional low-gravity duration (up to 10s by free-floating the apparatus), as well as an experimental package incorporating rainbow schlieren (which cannot be contained within a package for the 2.2-s drop tower), although radiative extinction was still not observed

. The unavoidable g-jitter associated with the facility, however, renders the observation less definitive. Note that even though the package was free-floated, umbilical restrictions could not be avoided. This g-jitter effect was substantiated by accelerometer data. 5-s drop tower experiments for a mixture composition of 20%H2 / 25%CH4 / 55%N2 did show events with local extinction toward the end of the drop (see Fig. 1.11). While these new results are extremely encouraging and suggest that radiative extinction can indeed be experimentally observed, the 5-s duration is still insufficient. To obtain spherical symmetry for small burners (in order to minimize heat loss to the burner), as well as to ensure quasi-steady flame evolution up to radiative extinction (for the flame sizes to be studied), low mass flow rates are needed, which increase the characteristic time needed. Moreover, for othe

r mixture compositions (such as 50%H2/10%CH4/40%N2 45%H2/55%N2), more than 5s of microgravity duration has been computationally predicted to be needed to achieve radiative extinction (see Fig. 1.12). Additional time is also needed to employ multi-staged flames (where the mass flow rate is changed) so that such phenomena as kinetic extinction can be studied (for example, by establishing a quasi-steady flame at a given flow rate and then reducing it so that the flame front moves inwardly and quasi-steadily until kinetic extinction). Finally, given the characteristic time for diffusion flame oscillation (see Fig. 1.14), which does not occur until the flame nears the quasi-steady extinction limits, extended microgravity duration becomes essential in order to study the phenomenon. 2.5.3 Justification for Space-Flight Facility As explained above, extended microgravity duration, of high quality

, is needed to make all necessary flame structure measurements, allowing for the study of transient phenomena (such as flame oscillations and fuel vapor accumulation) and extinction processes. Moreover, at present, the advanced diagnostics found on the space-flight facility cannot be utilized in the drop tower facilities. Numerical simulations indicate that about 25s of microgravity is needed for nonextinguishing flames to reach 80% of their steady-state radius, for the fuel mixtures and flow rates examined. It is expected that within this duration, the aforementioned phenomenon can be duly investigated. The total experimental duration for a single case would be 25s. This duration is within the 25s bound imposed by constant volume combustion within the specified CIR dimensions (see §Appendix 5.1) regarding oxygen depletion for a “penetration depth” of 20cm.

C. Science Objectives The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.1) of the experiment’s SRD from Jan. 2010. Current experimental and theoretical capabilities make detailed, quantitative descriptions of laminar flames situated in well-defined flow fields conceivable provided that comprehensive 5

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 chemical-kinetic and transport mechanisms are available. The comprehensiveness of these mechanisms has been extensively tested for premixed but not diffusion flames, especially in simple, well-defined flow fields not complicated by buoyant flows. A burner-generated spherical diffusion flame provides a simple, one-dimensional flame geometry that permits a rigorous comparison between detailed theory and experimental verification. Existing theory and limited low-gravity experimental results suggest that quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames can exist with some combinations of fuel mixture supply rates and quiescent ambient oxidizers. With respect to the steady flame conditions, altering fuel supply rates to limit flame residence time induces a convective-kinetic extinction limit. Alternatively, very large residence times allow radiative heat l

osses and diffusive transport mechanisms to quench the flame. Near these dual flammability boundaries of quasi-steady flames, flame-front instabilities may appear before the flame is quenched. We seek to investigate and improve the fidelity and comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic mechanisms and transport submodels used in the simulation of aerothermochemical phenomena, and consequently identify possible modifications, by characterizing important unit combustion processes, including: (1) the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames, with emphases on fuel vapor accumulation, radiation heat transfer, flame pulsation, and flame kinetics; and (2) the structure and response of characteristically sooty flames, with emphases on flame front stability and soot formation. Comprehensive predictive capability can be achieved by employing the simple flames of Process (1) to interrogate and su

ggest modifications of the kinetic and transport data bases, and then validate their adequacy in the chemically and aerodynamically more complex situation of Process (2). A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence): Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic exti

ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downli

Lightemitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniq

ues of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. B. Hardware Shortcomings Key s-Flame shortcomings include image acquisition, limited imaging sensitivity (especially to the hydrogen flames), and the flow asymmetry from the burner (especially at high flow rates). Other shortcomings are discussed in this section and Appendices B to D, but the reader may want to refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document for additional information. At high flow rates, the porous spherical burner used for s-Flame did not produce spherically symmetric flames. While they were nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center became increasing offset from the burner center when testing with higher flow rates. More specifically, the flame shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the sintered sphere. In other words, the flow from the bu

rner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. When s-Flame’s first fuel bottle was installed on 30 July 2019 (19211), it was at the expected pressure, but the fuel pressure was observed to drop with time, indicating a leak. Troubleshooting, including testing with other fuel bottles, was carried out and it was concluded that the leak was related to the bottle’s quick connection and potentially caused by foreign debris. The bottle was returned to Earth unused and tested in the ground copy of the CIR, but a leak was not found in that ground testing. As a result of this anomaly, testing with a planned hydrogen/methane/nitrogen blend was not accomplished.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 When a fuel or diluent Mass Flow Controller (MFC) was used at a small fraction of its maximum flow rate, the actual flow rate sometimes differed from that desired. More importantly, small flow perturbations were observed in some s-Flame tests, where the flow irregularities were most apparent through their effect on Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence. For example, a momentary increase in fuel flow, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. Steps were made to mitigate such behavior, e.g., by zero-ing the MFCs prior to each test, but they were not completely successful. Ignition of the flames in the second round, with helium rather than nitrogen dilution, presented a challenge. The properties of the two gases differ dramatically; for example, helium’s thermal conductivity is several times gre

ater than that of nitrogen. A cautious approach was taken in increasing the igniter power on the first test day with helium (11 May 2020, i.e., 20132) because of concerns about potential failure of the igniter tip and the stalled operations that would result. The number of tests accomplished with that day’s conditions were limited as a result. The standard igniter tip was subsequently replaced with a replaced with a coil, rather than loop, design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker wire. The coil igniter was used successfully in subsequent testing, but still with caution where flames were not always ignited successfully. As a result, some tests with helium dilution were conducted in atmospheres with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%, which as one would expect facilitated ignition. As a result, tests were conducted with an inconsistent mix of oxyg

en concentrations, which may yield valuable insights, but limits the planned test-to-test comparisons. The CIR’s Image Processing and Storage Unit for Gigabit Ethernet cameras (IPSU-G), which is used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, didn’t properly archive all of the image data on 13 Sept. 2019 (19256), where a large fraction of the image data was lost while flames were burning. After troubleshooting attempts, the IPSU-G was removed and replaced by astronaut Jessica Meir on 24 October 24 (19297) where subsequent check-out on Oct. 28 (19301) confirmed normal archival of the image data. The DataCam images were mis-formatted on 18 Dec. 2019 (19352), where the cause is unknown but there were repeated operational issues with the CIR’s Image Processing and Storage Units (IPSUs) on that test day. Fortunately, the mis-formatting was not

seen on subsequent test days and the problematic test day was nominally repeated on 24 Jan. 2020 (20024) to make up for the lost science. The ACME DataCam, generally the primary camera for ACME testing, is unfortunately not as sensitive as had been hoped to the dim microgravity flames. A critical challenge for s-Flame was in imaging the pure hydrogen and diluted hydrogen flames, which were not apparent or hardly visible to the DataCam and analog operations camera. This unfortunately inhibits assessment of three-dimensional flame symmetry because the CFI intensified camera and Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) cameras were opposite of each other. While infrequent, tests also sometimes aborted automatically, typically due to communication issues with an IPSU but sometimes because test parameters were accidentally assigned out-ofrange values. Fortunately, such aborts occurred before the

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 In contrast, a combination of factors led to testing being cut short on 3 June 2020 (20155). A high pressure reading (for a carrier gas) in the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) put the Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) Control Unit, i.e. the FCU, in an offnominal state. Rebooting the FCU inadvertently set the valve safety timers to zero, and they cannot be reset without venting and refilling the combustion chamber with the intended atmosphere. Those issues combined with an extended loss of commanding prevented further science operations on that day. However, a test day was added on 8 July 2020 (20190) to make up for the lost science.

Summary of Preliminary Results The s-Flame experiment aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well-defined flow fields such that the phenomena of interest can be studied without being complicated by various flow field effects. The basic flame configuration adopted for the investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing atmosphere in microgravity. The theoretically one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The s-Flame experiment uses the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the ACME hardware in the Destiny module of the ISS. Specifically, the s-Flame tests are intended to: (i) Advance our abilit

y to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames; (ii) Obtain experimental data in simple, well-defined flow fields and understand various key elemental diffusion flame processes; (iii) Identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damköhler numbers, respectively); (iv) Determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number; (v) Validate and/or improve accuracy of computational simulation including detailed chemistry and transport. The project has completed two (2) rounds of microgravity experimentation. Currently, detailed analyses of the acquired data, computational simulation, and theoretical analysis are ongoing. Interpretation of all

phenomena will emphasize the simultaneous and coupled influence of chemistry and transport. Table 1, on the preceding page, summarizes the tests conducted for two rounds of tests, which are meant to address the scientific objectives listed above. All experimental data address transient phenomenon, as the flame evolves from localized ignition towards “steady” behavior. The flames then evolve in a quasi-steady state manner (becoming history independent), after a short initial transient. Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene are used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon, and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with f

uel include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities and characteristic flame temperature. The rationale for the matrix of tests is to utilize various mixtures to assess both chemical and transport effects (including radiative) on flame behavior. Pure H2 and pure CH4 are utilized to assess kinetic mechanisms associated with each. Additionally, pure H2 only produces H2O as its radiative product, thereby isolating its radiative properties. Mixtures composed of both H2 and CH4 are used to examine their combined chemical and transport effects. N2 and He inerts which affect characteristic flame temperature and transport (molecular and radiative), in the same mole 25

Test day 19254 examines nitrogen-diluted C2H4 issuing into 21% O2 / 79% N2 atmosphere. C2H4 allows for the examination of a fuel with nominal unity Le number, setting a baseline standard for flame stretch and thermal diffusive stability effects. Additionally, its characteristic sooting nature (in normal gravity) directly addresses our basic science objectives focusing on spreading of flame sheets, dual extinction states, and flame-front instabilities. For a case of fuel-mixture of 20% C2H4 / 80% N2 at a flow rate of 3 cc/s, a seemingly quasi-steady flame is attained for extended duration. For the same mixture, higher flow rates of 5-10 cc/s result in radiative extinctions, corre

Soot is only observed during ignition, which goes away as the flames establish themselves, as seen for cases where low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) are ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). Nevertheless, comparisons with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction behavior. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction, making the chamber size an important parameter. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to observe for the conditions examined. Ignition was also severely affected by using He as diluent. es that are theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. However, such instabilities were not conclusively observed in the ISS tests, at least from the video images. Radiometer and PMT data will need to be examined in detail. (7) The highly thermal conductive nature of He seems to affect various processes, such as ignition and heat transfer to the burner (affecting isolation of kinetic extinction), despite higher characteristic flame temperatures. (8) Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity).

E. Accomplishment of Approved Objectives The ISS experimental matrix was proposed to address the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames. Comparisons with detailed computational simulation will permit assessment of transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence). The accomplishment aspect is given after the statement of each objective. Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. Transient flames, both expanding and contracting, were achieved for all fuel mixtures. Some flames appeared to be quasi-steady in their evolution from a non-steady ignition origin.

Transient sooting only occurred during forced ignition; however, the ignition process and associated phenomena are being analyzed. Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen cases may have indicated kinetic extinction, but more analyses are needed. Helium-diluted hydrogen/methane blends may have shown radiative extinction, but more analyses are needed. F. Additional Objectives Achieved No additional objectives have yet to be achieved. However, as we analyze and interpret the data, we expect new discoveries and insights into the fundamental mechanisms. Computational simulations will augment some test cases, and comparisons with experimental data will allow for extraction of basic parameters and assessment of chemical kinetic mechanisms. The role of the inerts will be better revealed, as the tests showed that they are far from passive participants in the flame dynamics and responses. Some additional objectives that may be achieved in the future would involve the following aspects given below. (A) Some experimental cases involved initial ramp up with subsequent ramp down in the flow rate, which may reveal hysteresis in the flame response. 31

G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of

understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters. In analyzing and validating the data sets, the experimental data and corresponding computational simulations should yield quantitative and qualitative understanding of various elemental flame phenomena. In studying the transient motion of diffusion flames ignited from a non-steady-state initial condition, the significance of fuel accumulation will be evaluated, which was originally found to be important in droplet burning. Here, with no droplet surface regression nor coupling of fuel flow to heat transfer from the flame to influence flame-front motion, the effect can be better isolated and the far-field unsteadiness assessed. Quantitative predictability of the flame motion permits assessment of the parameters and mechanisms involved in radiation loss and reabsorption as well as

other transport parameters. The microgravity environment greatly facilitates the examination of pulsating instabilities, which can be hidden or coupled to other processes in normal gravity. Moreover, involvement of multi-dimensional effects, rather than the nominally 1-D geometry here, would further complicate the manifestation of the phenomenon. Near-limit phenomena, including extinction, is best evaluated and validated using our onedimensional spherical diffusion flame (as realized in the microgravity environment), which is probably the most desirable flame configuration for study of this nature. Understanding extinction phenomenon is paramount to revealing basic flame processes, along with highlighting implications in fire safety. The results are of strong interest to other groups working on diffusion flames, including those also doing ISS-based experiments. The main products will be

(i) insights from fundamental characterization of transient dynamics and responses of such flames, (ii) categorization of processes that are either quasi-steady (e.g., expanding flame front motion toward steady state) or fully transient (e.g., pulsating instabilities prior to extinction), (iii) quantitative and qualitative mapping of extinction boundaries and unstable regimes, (iv) clarification of the role of diluents in various processes, and (v) additional understanding of ignition in non-premixed flames. Engines and devices on Earth can be improved in efficiency, pollutant emissions, and dependability from such products.

Follow-On Experiments Although two rounds of testing have been completed, with no further testing planned, if a third round becomes available, there are two main types of experiments that we would like to implement. We would like to examine the same fuel mixtures (plus C3H8 as mentioned below) of the first two rounds, but with CO2 as inert, including that for the ambient. N2 and He are radiatively transparent gases; while CO2 is an optically participating gas. Use of CO2 should result in a characteristically lower flame temperature, increasing the Zeldovich number, Ze. At the same time, the highly reabsorptive CO2 species can minimize net radiative heat loss affecting flame dynamics and extinction. Objectives A, B, and C would be addressed by these experiments. Additionally, characteristically sooty flames were not observed in the first tw

o rounds for the fuel mixtures tested. As such, we would like to investigate using C3H8 as fuel, which was originally specified in the SRD that was approved [in 2002, but which was not part of the s-Flame plan under ACME, which didn’t begin until 2006]. Specific knowledge originally sought in the first two rounds with respect to sooty flames, which were not achieved consist of: (a) the transient and steady state behavior and structure of sooting spherical flames, (b) residence time effect on soot formation, with only curvature effects and no strain, and (c) the effects of soot radiation and transport on extinction, at constant mass flow rate. The results so far will be compared with computational simulations to address deficiencies in fundamental parameters and models. The aforementioned CO2 experiments are highly desired; however, experimentation with C3H8 is of utmost importance if we
are to achieve our original objectives with respect to characteristically sooty flames, which were not attained for the fuel mixtures and conditions tested in the first two rounds.

Introduction Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for impro

ved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The spherical flames are ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally toward extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from heat loss or is blown out, respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of 37

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures. More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). A. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze),

onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the

detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify anal

ysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. 38

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s-Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be c

onducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. But it is not expected that such control, which might be used to approach a stability or soot limit, will be used for s-Flame. Thus far, that has been the case for this experiment, with the possible mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Note that the investigation’s science testing didn’t begin until September 2019, so no flames were ignited during Increment 59. The s-Flame experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including hydrogen, methane, hydrogen/methane blends, and ethylene. These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is relatively well understood. The Increment 60 tests were all conducted with ethylene (C2H4), which is typically highly sooting because of its carbon double bond, but where the fuel was diluted with nitrogen for these tests. 39

Mission anomalies When s-Flame’s first fuel bottle was installed on the CIR on July 30 (19211) it was at the expected pressure, but the fuel pressure was observed to drop with time, indicating a leak. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-sphe

rical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. E. Preliminary Research Findings The s-Flame experiment utilizes spherically-symmetric diffusion flames and their dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction, instability, and soot formation. ISS testing for 19254 and 19256 examined nitrogendiluted ethylene flames in air. The experiments of 19254 revealed that a quasi-steady flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3cc/s for 20% C2H4 / 80% N2. The flame was shut down by the automated system because the burner reached a cut-off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame oscillated near the end of the experiment, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For higher flow rates, e.g., 5-10cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were observed. Generally, the flames showed unst

able behavior near the burner tube prior to extinction, likely because of lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4 / 75% N2 and 30% C2H4 / 70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame, allowing extraction of temperature in on-going analyses. Soot was observed only during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To asses whether these nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at

high flow rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our ground-based experiments, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions. The experiments of 19256 were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp down 43

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain a quasisteady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up cases were also examined. Introduction Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for impro

ved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The spherical flames are ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames. One experimental objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame 46

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out,” respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions. More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) fo

r mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). B. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions. As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the motion (e.g., expansion) of sphe

rical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are

increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low 47

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s-Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of t

he testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. But it is not expected that such control, which might be used to approach a stability or soot limit, will be used for s-Flame. Thus far, that has been the case for this experiment, with the possible mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

The s-Flame experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including hydrogen, methane, hydrogen/methane blends, and ethylene. These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is relatively well understood. The Increment 60 tests were all 48

Mission anomalies The only significant anomaly to occur during this increment pair was the misformatting of image data from ACME’s primary camera on Dec. 18 (19352). The cause is unknown, but there were repeated operational issues with the CIR’s Image Processing and Storage Units (IPSUs) on that test day. During testing on Sept. 13 (19256), the CIR’s IPSU-G Image Processing and Storage Unit for Gigabit Ethernet cameras, which is used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, didn’t properly archive all of the image data on Sept. 13 (19256). A large fraction of the image data was lost. The issue wasn’t resolved by remote trouble shooting and the IPSU-G was ultimately removed and replaced by astronaut Jessica Meir on October 24 (19297). Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data Neglecting the anomalies, the most noteworthy challenge was

in imaging the hydrogen and hydrogen-diluted flames, which were not apparent or hardly visible to the operations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera for ACME testing. The testing with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted on Dec. 18 (19352) and Jan. 24 (20024), where the testing on the latter day was to make up for the earlier image mis-formatting discussed in the preceding section. This situation unfortunately inhibits assessment of the three-dimensional flame symmetry as the two intensified cameras are opposite of each other. During Increment 61, several s-Flame tests automatically aborted (due to the controlling software script), where that was prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME experiments. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. ACME aborts norma

lly occur because of communication issues with an IPSU, and that happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20024N1, and 20024J1. A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013C2. ACME aborts are infrequent, but there are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here. Tests are also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite, where that occurred during Increment 61 in tests 19304A4, 19304A6, 19308C1, and 20006A1. That can be corrected by adjusting various test parameters and other settings. In this case, adjustments were subsequently made to the ignition position (e.g., after 19304A4 and 19304A6), the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation (e.g., after 19308C1), and the duration of the igniter activation (e.g., after

20006A1). As another example, failed ignition can result from false ignition detection and deactivation resulting from the combination of settings for ignition and detection, e.g., the gain for the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module measuring the OH* chemiluminescence. The latter, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. 50

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed

from that desired. However, this was not a surprise to those familiar with the hardware. Flow perturbations have been noticed in some s-Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always performed satisfactorily. In tests conducted using the 1-slpm fuel MFC (where the flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has been seen to overshoot and undershoot when first opening. Small flow irregularities have been most apparent through their effect on the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence. A momentary increase in fuel flow, as has occurred in some s-Flame tests, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. The MFCs are tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are typically made to (1) the setting that controls when the valves open and (2) the Propo

rtional-IntegralDerivative (PID) settings. This ACME activity has involved significant testing, where there are an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gas types. While the MFC adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems. It was seen in prior ACME testing that nitrogen oscillations (if any) tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow can be used so that such oscillations might end before the flame is ignited. As another measure, the MFCs are re-zeroed prior to each test, where that was another measure adopted in earlier ACME testing.

Different radii are being considered and plotted together, as some flames are not completely symmetric.
