E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by Prof. Tse and lightly edited by Stocker] The s-Flame experiment utilizes spherically-symmetric diffusion flames and their dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction, instability, and soot formation. The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20% C2H4/80% N2 (on a volume basis). The flame was shut down by the automated system because the burner reached a cut-off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For higher flow rates, e.g., 5-10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were 52

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to extinction, likely because of lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame, allowing determination of temperature in on-going analyses. Soot was observed only during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extingui

shed, but no sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our groundbased studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions. The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished

. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp up before reaching 8 cc/s. Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere. The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore, larger flow

rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, characteristically larger flames would be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitrogen-diluted methane flames were planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2. Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen-diluted methane flames in 30% O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% down to 15% were examined. For 45% CH4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and 9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extinguished. These flames 53

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction. For 30% CH4/70% N2, flow rates of 3, 5, and 10 cc/s produced flames that expanded to extinction (assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 3 to 1 cc/s resulted in presumably kinetic extinction during ramp down. For 25% CH4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of 10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp down, suggesting kinetic extinction. For 15% CH4/85% N2, flames were ignited, but extinguished very quickly. These tests of 19308 suggest that they could mani

fest both radiative and kinetic extinction for the conditions specified. The 19352 tests examined various concentrations of H2 (45%-70%) diluted with N2 issuing into air. The installed fuel MFC had a maximum output of 0.1 slpm, which unfortunately provided a less-than-sufficient flow range where its use may have precluded the study of radiative extinction corresponding to larger flame sizes. Imaging the diluted hydrogen flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam were mis-formatted. Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g., where it, like the DataCam and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, cannot image the ultraviolet OH* flame emission (at 310 nm). Analysis of images from the Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera and its OH* filter is ongoing. And as one might expect, little could be seen with the CFI

intensified camera using its broadband CH2O filter. Quasi-steady flames seem to be present at low flow rates (e.g., 2.4 cc/s for 70% H 2), as inferred from PMT, pyrometry fiber emission, and burner temperature observations. Kinetic extinction seems to occur as the flow rate is ramped down. There were various problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H2 bottle with a higher flow rate MFC was later performed for tests of 20024 (see below), which was a make-up test day added because of the mis-formatting of the DataCam image files. The tests conducted 20006, using the 44.4% H2/55.6% CH4 bottle, examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Flames extinguished, some with wavy oscillating behavior prior to extinction. However, it seems that even for very small flow rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction was by the radiative mechanism during flame expansion. There was

too little parameter room in terms of flow rate and burner size to identify conclusively kinetic extinction during ramp down for these mixtures. In short, radiative extinction (with local flame extinction and re-ignition seemed to occur prior to ultimate extinguishment) during flame expansion after ignition was observed. However, it is unclear whether ramping down the flow rate resulted in kinetic extinction. Detailed analyses of the data are needed. The various cameras seemed to capture the tests well. The 20013 tests, which used the 66.7% H2/33.3% CH4 bottle, mainly investigated 30% H2/15% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Radiative extinction was difficult to identify conclusively because flames with larger flow rates, e.g. 15 cc/s, seemed to last, although with patchy extinction areas, until time out. Larger flow rates could not be examined 54

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 either because of limited MFC range or distorted flame shape cause by burner limitations at high flow rates. Also, kinetic extinction during ramp down could not be identified conclusively, as some flames seemed to extinguish because they were "going into the burner." The 20024 tests using the 100% H2 bottle repeated and augmented conditions for those of 19352 where the 0.1-slpm fuel MFC range was too low to examine radiative extinction and the analog and intensified cameras did not pick up the flame images at all or well. Here, the 0.5-slpm fuel MFC was used and only a fused silica filter was used for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera. 45%-15% H2/N2 balance mixtures were investigated. The flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing quasi-steady until time out. The pyrometry fibers glowed, perha

ps making good flamestructure measurements, which will be evaluated subsequently. The flames seemed to extinguish during ramp down, but further analysis is needed to assess kinetic extinction. The tests conducted on 20029 used 50% C2H4/50% N2 and repeated and augmented conditions of 19256, when the images were not good. Again, the results indicated both kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions. However, no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C2H4 and an enriched oxygen atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests. In summary, selected preliminary findings from this testing include: o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow rates. As previously mentioned above (and in our report for the preceding

increment pair), such phenomena were not observed in our ground-based research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction behavior. o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated, radiative extinction was not observed. o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested extinction, which are presumed to be radiative. However, kinetic extinction at low flow rates could not be identified. More analyses of the data are needed. Early ISS results were presented in the following presentations: 1. Chung K. One experimental objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out,” respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions. 57

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically pred

icted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions. As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the develo

pment of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity

to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to 58

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s-Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. As expected, no s-Flame tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a c

ontrol parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Mission anomalies While there were certainly issues with testing discussed in the next section, there were no significant anomalies during s-Flame’s Increment 63 testing. However, anomalies did occur during Increment 60 and 61 which led to corrective actions and/or make-up testing. 2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this increment. All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in Increments 60 and 61. The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making comparison testing very desirable for manifestation of dif

ferent phenomena. Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen, so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames. The power level was slowly increased from test to test until ignition was finally achieved on the ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11 (20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63. The cautious approach was taken because of concerns that the igniter tip might fail (i.e., burn out) if too much power was applied. An igniter failure would have likely halted testing for weeks given the need to schedule the commander’s time to replace the igniter tip. After that first test day, the decision was made to have the igniter replaced with a coil rather than loop design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker wire. Furthermore, the igniter tip had not be

en replaced in months, and the tips do degrade with time, especially when they are not quickly retracted from the ignited flames. The coil igniter was used successfully but still with caution, where flames were not always ignited successfully. Subsequently, some tests were conducted in atmosphere with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%. As one would expect, that proved to be helpful for achieving ignition. But the end result was that some tests were conducted with 21% oxygen, some at 30%, and some at both nominal concentrations. Fortuitously, this mixture of conditions may provide deeper insight into the mechanisms of flame dynamics and response. Tests are also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite, where that occurred, for example, during Increment 61 in tests 19304A4, 19304A6, 19308C1, and 20006A1. That can be corrected by adjusting various test parameters and ot

her settings. In this case, adjustments were subsequently made to the ignition position (e.g., after 19304A4 and 19304A6), the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation (e.g., after 19308C1), and the duration of the igniter activation (e.g., after 20006A1). As another example, failed ignition can result from false ignition detection and 61

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 deactivation resulting from the combination of settings for ignition and detection, e.g., the gain for the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module measuring the OH* chemiluminescence. The latter, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. Testing on June 3 (20155) was cut short due to a combination of issues. The final test was aborted due to an error with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU). Consoles needed to be reset for the new increment, and there was an issue with the Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) Control Unit, i.e. the FCU. Rebooting the FCU inadvertently set the valve safety timers to zero, which cannot be reset without venting and refilling the combustion chamber with the intended atmosphere. Those issu

es combined with an extended loss of commanding prevented further science operations on that day. Therefore, an additional test day (July 8, i.e., 20190) was added to make up for lost science, e.g., where only one test was successfully conducted at ~21% oxygen on June 3. The FCU was off nominal because of a high carrier gas pressure in the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). Imaging of the hydrogen flames was often an issue, where they were not apparent or hardly visible to the operations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera for ACME testing. The testing with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted on Dec. 18 (19352), Jan. 24 (20024), June 3 (20155), and July 8 (20190). This shortcoming unfortunately inhibits assessment of the three-dimensional flame symmetry as the two intensified cameras were opposite of each other.

The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints. At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally que

nches near the supply tube. When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. However, this was not a surprise to those familiar with the hardware. Flow perturbations have been noticed in some s-Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always 62

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 performed satisfactorily. In tests conducted using the 1-slpm fuel MFC (where the flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has been seen to overshoot and undershoot when first opening. Small flow irregularities have been most apparent through their effect on the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence. A momentary increase in fuel flow, as has occurred in some s-Flame tests, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. The MFCs are tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are typically made to (1) the setting that controls when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-IntegralDerivative (PID) settings. This ACME activity has involved significant testing, where there is an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gas types. While the MFC a

djustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems. It was seen in prior ACME testing that nitrogen oscillations (if any) tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow can be used so that such oscillations might end before the flame is ignited. As another measure, the MFCs are re-zeroed prior to each test, where that was another measure adopted in earlier ACME testing. As mentioned previously, s-Flame tests have sometimes automatically aborted (because of the controlling software script), where that is normally prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME experiments. As a result, there was little lost other than the available experimental time in the failed test attempt. ACME aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an IPSU, which for example happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20024N1, an

d 20024J1. A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included for example 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013C2. ACME aborts are infrequent, but there are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here.

C. Completeness/Quality of Data During Increments 60 and 61, nine days of tests were conducted during which 145 flames were ignited for the first round of testing. In contrast, only 29 tests were specified as required or highly desired in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) for that round. Therefore, a wealth of data was obtained for this round of testing which featured gaseous fuels diluted by nitrogen. However, there was a significant loss of data. Most importantly, the first fuel bottle appeared to leak on installation (in Increment 60) and later on-orbit testing (in Increment 61) with other hydrogen/methane blends suggests that its fuel mixture would have been ideal for achieving science success. Furthermore, there was significant image data loss on two different test days, specifically Sept. 13 (19256) and Dec. 18 (19352). As a result, those test days were nomin

ally repeated on Jan. 29 (20029) and Jan. 24 (20024), respectively (i.e., in a reversed order). For these reasons, a simple comparison of the total number of flames ignited (145) with that specified as required or highly desired (29) for the first round of testing is somewhat misleading. 63

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 As discussed in the preceding section, the hydrogen and diluted-hydrogen flames were not apparent or extremely dim in imaging from the operations camera and ACME DataCam. Neglecting that factor, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).

D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by Prof. Stephen Tse, Rutgers U.] Image files are currently being processed. Radial positions of maximum CH* chemiluminescence is being plotted against time. Different radii are being considered and plotted together, as some flames are not completely symmetric. MFC and PMT data are being compared with video images to assess and confirm experimental settings. Radiometer data is being reviewed. Analyses of the fiber pyrometry data are ongoing. MATLAB code is used to isolate fiber images, which are then color assessed for temperature. Computational simulations with detailed chemistry and transport of the test cases are underway. Time-dependent simulations will be compared with the time-dependent experimental data, where tracking of the flamefront location is based on chemiluminescent emission. Steady-state simulations will produce the Isola curves mappin

g flame response versus system Damkhöler number for given fuel mixtures. The experimental cases will then be pin-pointed on the computational mappings to assess whether the experimental conditions are in quasi-steady state or near extinction limits, either kinetic or radiative. Oscillation behavior will be correlated to possible pulsating oscillations found in the simulations.

E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by Prof. Tse and lightly edited by Stocker] The s-Flame experiment utilizes spherically-symmetric diffusion flames and their dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction, instability, and soot formation. The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20% C2H4/80% N2 (on a volume basis). The flame was shut down by the automated system because the burner reached a cut-off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For higher flow rates, e.g., 5-10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were observed. Generally,

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame, allowing determination of temperature in on-going analyses. Soot was observed only during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our gro

undbased studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions. The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain a quasi-stea

dy flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp up before reaching 8 cc/s. Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere. The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore, larger flow rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, characteristically larger flames woul

d be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitrogen-diluted methane flames were planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2. Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen-diluted methane flames in 30% O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% down to 15% were examined. For 45% CH4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and 9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extinguished. These flames appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction. For 30% 65

For 25% CH4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of 10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp down, suggesting kinetic extinction. Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling. Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At 5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner temperature limit. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s, minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. For tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded to extinction. At 4 cc/s, the flame lasted a while before eventual extinction. The 3 cc/s case did not ignite. Ramp down of the flow rate seemed to res

ult in flames that extinguished quickly before the protocol could ramp down the flow rate. The last testing of Round 2, which was a makeup of 20155, occurred on 20190, with 45% H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. For both oxygen concentration environments, flow rates resulting in expanding flames lasted for a while, but were cut off by automated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was observed for both oxygen concentration environments. We are currently analyzing the data to determine if extinction was kinetic or due to heat loss to the burner. A last set of tests were conducted with a reduced oxygen concentration atmosphere, i.e., 17.5% O2/82.5% He. Some cases indicated that radiative and kinetic extinction were possibly observed. In summary, selected prelimina

ry findings from this testing include: o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow rates. As previously mentioned above (and in our report for the preceding increment pair), such phenomena were not observed in our ground-based research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction behavior. 69

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) o o o 29 July 2021 Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated, radiative extinction was not observed. Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested extinction, which are presumed to be radiative. However, kinetic extinction at low flow rates could not be identified. More analyses of the data are needed. Cases for helium-diluted cases shifted the extinction limits with respect to the nitrogen-diluted cases. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to observe for the conditions examined. More analyses are needed to assess instability near the flame limits, which was predicted to occur computationally.

Methane ignition hadn’t been an issue in earlier testing with nitrogen dilution, but it was challenging in this week’s tests because of helium’s much greater thermal conductivity. Nonetheless, the recently installed coiled igniter tip enabled us to ignite these flames. The results from the current series of s-Flame tests will be compared with the results from the previous tests using nitrogen dilution. In that earlier testing, it was found that radiative extinction (i.e., extinction caused by radiative heat loss) is a common event, which had been predicted computationally. However, w

e did not observe this in preliminary ground-based testing. It was also seen in the on-orbit tests that radiative reabsorption extends the flame size at extinction. It will be interesting to see what the future comparisons will reveal about the nature of flames. The flame becomes all blue and retreats from the fuel supply tube because of heat loss. This mixing enhances flammability and the reinvigorated and locally brighter flame flashes back to the supply tube reestablishing the nominally spherical flame. But it is short-lived, and the flame quickly retreats again until it is just a “cap” on the left. Mixing again leads to another flame flash, but it quickly extinguishes due to radiative heat loss, heat loss to the supply tube, and conductive heat loss enhanced by the helium’s high thermal conductivity.

Week 11: June 19 - 25 On GMT 170, 20 flames were ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). These flames burned a 25% ethylene/75% helium blend; whereas, the flames on GMT 164 burned a 20% ethylene/80% helium blend. Comparing these data will enable analysis of the effects of this fuel/inert blend on flame dynamics, such as extinction behavior and structure. On GMT 171, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points using a 30% ethylene/70% helium blend. ACME s-Flame Test Point Image

25% 20% In this image (preliminary and false-colored), the flame on the right has a higher ethylene concentration than the flame on the left. As expected, the flame on the right is larger where the spherical flame expands until the fuel reaches enough oxygen to be consumed. These flames, which are non-premixed, are like bubbles in that the gaseous fuel is inside the bubble and the oxygen is outside the bubble. The flame shell, like the film of a bubble, is a thin sheet where the fuel and oxygen come together and react, producing light, heat, and chemical products, such as carbon dioxide and water vapor. Meanwhile, the helium—which readily diffuses—is free to cross the flame shell.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 However, diffusion was minimal because the helium concentrations within the fuel and the surrounding atmosphere were similar. Both flames were bright and sooty at ignition, but these images are from late in each test when the flames became dim. The bright lines at the top are the 14-micron ceramic fibers used for optical determination of the flame temperature using a camera characterized for that purpose. s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth.

Week 12: June 26 - July 2 GMT 176 was a record-breaking day for ACME with 23 flames ignited—the most we’ve ignited in one day! We’ve now ignited over 250 flames for s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) and over 1000 flames for ACME since it started in Nov. 2017. The tests on GMT 176 were performed with 30% ethylene in helium for comparison with the results from the two preceding test days, which burned 20% and 25% ethylene/helium blends. CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG In this test point video, helium-diluted ethylene fuel is ignited with a low fuel flow rate to limit the soot produced with ignition. After ignition, the flow rate is tripled in a smooth ramp, so that the flame response can be observed. As expected, the flame quickly grows, where it must expand to reach enough oxygen to consume all the fuel. Before the fuel flow rate has comple

tely tripled, the flame retreats from the burner’s fuel supply tube because of heat loss—creating a hole in the flame near the tube. This hole allows for increased mixing of the ethylene and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame shell. This mixing causes the flame to momentarily reestablish around the burner tube with a bright flash of light. Mixing again leads to another flame flash, after which the flame fully extinguishes. The fuel flow rate did completely triple before the flame extinguished. Although not visible in the video, the measured OH* and CH* chemiluminescence was relatively constant throughout this test with the important exceptions of ignition and the bright flashes of light prior to extinction. In contrast, the measured chemiluminescence declined with time in similar tests with constant fuel flow rates. OH* and CH* are molecules at an elevated energy state whi

ch emit a photon of a specific wavelength as their energy level drops a level. The CH* emission is the source of most of the blue in a hydrocarbon flame, while the OH* emission is in the ultraviolet. ACME uses the latter measurement as an indicator of ignition and extinction because it is insensitive to the hot-wire igniter and hot burned gases. Using this unique microgravity data, the s-Flame investigation seeks to test and improve computational models, which may enable improvements to practical combustion on Earth.

To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The s-Flame image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used with CH*, formaldehyde, and UV fused silica filters, but where only a single filter was used in each test 3. Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera, equipped with an OH* filter 4. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination

package, which was sometimes left off The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, HiBMs, and LLL-UV cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

1. Overview The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.” Cool flames are controlled by low temperature chemistry, and occur in the NTC region of n-alkane fuels. FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K. Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure and temperature, three different fuel combinations were investigated, namely, pure n-dodecane, n-dodecane/isododecane mixtures and farnesane ( a renewable jet fuel) at ambient pre

ssures up to 5 atmospheres. Cool flame extinction occurs when its static stability is lost close to the lower turnover point in the NTC region, addition of helium to the ambient gas is also considered. Results for droplet burning rates, flame dynamics, droplet extinction diameters, and flame radiant out put are measured. 2. Introduction (PS): Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day which averages out to an astonishing 2.5 gallons per day per person (Reitz, 2013). The primary reasons for such a high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but globally, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability compared to many other forms of energy. With the emergence

of newer internal combustion engine technologies such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Reactivity-Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines, understanding the autoignition and heat release chemistry and kinetics of hydrocarbon fuels is more important that ever. These new technologies coupled with the emergence of major sources of renewable fuels for both gasoline and diesel applications, including butanols and heavier alcohols, bio-diesel, farnesane and high carbon number synthetics, further emphasize the need to understand the kinetic effects of blending renewables with petroleum derived fuels. a. Objectives Cool flame phenomena are influenced by a number of factors, including the fuel molecular structure (for pure fuel cases), the ambient environment (pressure, temperature, oxygen and diluent (He) concentrations), and the fuel composition (the mixture of fuel

structures and perhaps fuel additives such as those used to change octane or cetane behavior). Though it is not possible to examine all of these factors in a thorough manner, here we propose a set of experiments that explore each one of these factors, namely, fuel structure effects, ambient conditions effect, fuel mixture effects, and the presence of fuel additives. 2

. Science Overview a. Background Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day, which averages out to an amazing 2.5 gallons per day per person. The primary reason for such high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but in the rest of the world, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability, compared to many other forms of energy sources. With the emergence of newer technologies for internal combustion engines and the increasing use of renewable bio-fuels, such as the Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engine and bio-diesel, that promise cleaner more efficient and sustainable utilization of hydrocarbon fuels, the need to understand the fundamenta

l chemical and physical aspects of liquid-fuel combustion is bound to increase. Commercially available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes being major components. The combustion characteristics of these alkanes are quite complex and follow branched-chain reaction pathways involving many intermediate radicals. The chemical pathways vary, depending on temperature and, to a lesser extent, on pressure. In general it is possible to identify a low-temperature reaction mechanism and a hightemperature mechanism, with a transition region between them. Many hydrocarbons exhibit a unique feature in this transition region, namely that the reaction rate decreases with increasing temperature, 3

leading it to be called the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) region. There area a number of models available in the literature, simplified chemical-kinetic model involving hundreds of reactions as well as detailed mechanisms involving thousands of reactions. Droplet-combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) conducted onboard the International Space Station, as part of the Flame Extinguishment Experiments, have revealed for the first time that large n-alkane droplets can continue to burn quasi-steadily in the NTC region (see, Fig 1). NTC behavior of the heat-release rate is necessary for low-temperature quasi-steady droplet burning to be stable. It was observed that the secondstage combustion of the droplet controlled by low-temperature NTC chemistry, referred to as ``cool-flame combustion" here for the sake of simplicity, abruptly ends at a finite droplet diameter, leaving the unburned
droplet to vaporize in the hot atmosphere. A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.

Figure 1. Three representative examples of radiative extinction and subsequent cool flame combustion of nheptane droplets in air. Inset shows the visible flame, backlit droplet images and the vapor cloud formation. Furthermore, the second-stage flame is shown to lie closer to the droplet surface where the rates of heat generation by the NTC chemistry is dynamically balanced by the heat loss rate. Unlike the hot-flame combustion where the overall process is controlled by equilibrium thermodynamic properties of the fuel, the cool-flame combustion depends on the chemical-kinetic details of the NTC region. These experimental and numerical studies provide a new tool to further explore the NTC chemistry of liquid fuels in an entirely new way. The experimental cool-flame droplet burning rates provide measures of the heat-release rates and stoichiometry, the flame-diameter evolution provides ins

ight into hot-flame diffusive and convective heat-loss effects, and the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic characteristic times. The objectives of the CFI experiments is to further explore the cool flame phenomenon using pure fuels, and fuel mixtures over a range of pressures and helium dilution. b. Rational for Microgravity (if unusual) 4

Rationale for microgravity remains the same for all the droplet combustion experiments conducted onboard the ISS. In microgravity the droplets burn in a spherically symmetric form, and therefore it is possible to model the processes with complex chemical kinetic mechanisms involving thousands of reactions leading to a better understanding of the chemistry. Moreover, the cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames. c. NRA the Investigation was Selected Under This project was initiated by NASA through a Science Definition Team (SDT) which formulated the overall objectives. It was peer reviewed by an independent panel of scientists and approved by NASA HQ as a follow-up experiments to FLEX, and FLEX-2 in the CIR using additional fuels and gases needed to complete the test matrix. The experimental hardware is same as

that of the FLEX experiments with few minor modifications in the data acquisition systems. d. Final Experiment Objectives Examine the cool flame combustion behavior of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane fuel mixtures, and farnesane fuels over a rage of pressure from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 4. Operations a. Procedures The operational procedure used in the CFI tests is the same as for the FLEX experiments. Once the ISS crew installs the required fuel syringe, and the gas bottles containing the gas mixtures in the MDCA and CIR facilities, all the actual experimental operations are conducted from the ground at the Telescience Support Center (TSC) located at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Prior to each test the combustion chamber is filled with the specified gas mixture at the required pressure, and the hot-wire igniters are positioned close to the droplet deployment site. Subsequently, a dropl

et of desired size is dispensed between the hypodermic needles and freely deployed, and ignited. The igniter is withdrawn from the FOV once ignition is detected. When required a 40 micron silicon-carbide fiber is used to tether the droplet at one place and stop it from drifting off from the field of view. The combustion process is recorded using a backlit, black-and-white camera ( 5 cm X 5 cm FOV) to obtain droplet size as a function of time, a UV-sensitive camera is used to image the OH* emission from the flame which provides the flame size data. A color camera which is had a live downlink to the TSC is used to perform and monitor the overall process. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers are used to measure the radiation emission from the flame. Details of the experimental hardware and the data reduction procedures can be found in Dietrich et al. (2014) b. On-Orbit Testing Over two hun

dred tests were carried out during the CFI experimental campaign. The initial droplet size was kept around 4 mm so that radiative extinction and the subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed. The list of experiments performed are as follows: • • • •

Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3, and 5 atm. N-dodecane/Iso-dodecane mixtures: 75/25% and 60/40% by mass at pressures from 0.5 to 5 atm Helium dilution by 29% and 59% with O2 mole fraction at 0.21 Farnesane: from 0.75 to 3 atm c. Anomalies That Effect Science Surprises/New Discovery No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed. This behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments. Furthermore, the soot-shell 5

which surrounds the droplet and lies between the droplet surface and the flame, became unstable and illdefined at higher pressures, a phenomenon which is not fully understood. d. Results a. Findings All the CFI data is yet to be fully analyzed and interpreted using theoretical and numerical models. A brief overview of general observations made during preliminary data analysis prior to posting on the PSI website is presented below. Interested researchers are welcome to propose to NASA for further analysis and interpretation of CFI data. 5.1 Cool flames: Cool flames were observed during n-dodecanol combustion as well as
n-dodecanol/iso-dodecanol mixture cases. The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol. Figure 1 shows a typical case of cool-flame behavior for n-dodecanol.

Figure 1. FLEX-1223: N-dodecane at 1.25 atm pressure in air. 5.2 Warm flames: Warm flames are a consequence of changing in chemical pathway during n-alkane oxidation. Figure 2 shows (Westbrook, 2010) the various chemical pathways: cool flames occur when low-temperature branching is dominant, when intermediate temperatures become more active warm flames are established. During warm flames the heat release rate dynamically balance the heat loss rate. Addition of helium seems to enhance this balance within the NTC region. 6

Figure 2. Chemical kinetic pathways for n-alkane oxidation (Westbrook, 2010). Figure 3: FLEX-1268 – N-dodecane at 3 atm burning in 12%O2 – 50% N2 – 29% Helium. Reignition and warm flame formation are shown. Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not visible in the color camera. Subsequently, a hot flame is ignited which quickly extinguishes to form a cool flame. 5.3 Cool flame extinction: 7

Cool flame extinction is controlled primarily by chemical kinetics. As the droplet size decreases, the residence time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction. Figure 4 shows the cool flame extinction diameter as function of ambient pressure for both free-floated and fiber-supported droplets for pure n-dodecane burning in air. As mentioned earlier, as the pressure is increased above approximately 2 atm, reignitions were commonly observed, eventually leading to complete combustion of the fuel droplet. It is interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter.

Figure 4. Cool flame extinction diameters as a function of ambient pressure for n-dodecane droplets burning in air. Since the cool flame extinction is an instability phenomenon where the dynamic balance between heat release and heat loss from the flame is lost at the lower turning point in the NTC region, one would expect addition of helium to have a substantial influence on the process. Figure 5 illustrates the effect of helium dilution on the extinction diameter for n-dodecane. Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger extinction diameter.

Figure 5. Effect of helium dilution on cool flame extinction during n-dodecane droplet combustion. 5.4 Sooting behavior as function of ambient pressure: The effects and the process of soot formation during cool flame combustion remains largely unexplored. The shoot shell that forms during hot flame is stabilized by the balance of force between fluid mechanical drag and the thermophoretic force. At low pressures a stable spherical soot-shell is formed. However, as the pressure increase the soot-shell becomes diffuse and undefined. The reasons for this phenomenon is still not well understood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame

Figure 6. Backlit images of the droplet during hot and cool flame burning at atmospheric pressures of approximately 380, 570, 760, 1520, 2280 and 3800 mmHg. The hot flame images are approximately 4 sec after igniter withdraw and the cool flame images are approximately 5 sec after hot flame extinction. The droplet in the cool flame image at 1520 mmHg was close to the edge of the FOV. The red circles during hot flame burning at the two highest pressures show the approximate location of the droplet surface. 5.5 Summary of findings: CFI experiments has provided cool flame burning data for pure n-dodecane, and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures. Farnesane, a commercially available renewable fuel characteristics were also studied. The effect of pressure and helium dilution were studied for these fuels. b. Benefits Low temperature chemistry is of fundamental importance in the combustion of many practical fuels. Low temperature chemistry controls the autoignition of fuels when injected into a combustion chamber, and in homogeneous mixtures of fuel and oxygen. New internal combustion engines, such as the HCCI engines, operate at low temperatures reducing the pollution formation and increasing overall efficiencies. The CFI experimental measurements provide a useful way to validate the complex chemical kinetic mechanisms that are being developed. The cool flame combustion process itself maybe of use in fuel reformulation technologies to produce hydrogen in fuel cell applications. c. Patents None 6. 1 Executive Summary This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke aerosol relative to smoke on Earth. We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about fluid/thermal/particle interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain, convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two flow rates, two geometric configurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity, buoyancy produces asymmetries in all fields of interest and amplifies vapor

-to-particle conversion near room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼ 40 µm and the mode particle size to ∼ 5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large particles (> 20 µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and smaller particles (< 10 µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large particle mode does not appear in microgravity flows that do not have prominent high temperature recirculation, although the aerosol still contains

large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle diameter in microgravity is ∼ 10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot, recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution. A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The final document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.

undamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two crossflow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation

and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar fields as a means to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle fields interact with the fluid dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, flow geometry, and the higher flow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize findings relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.

mixture); the particle velocity equals the fluid velocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the domain (including the large particles). • The fluid and particles are in thermal equilibrium and have the same temperature. • Particle diffusion coefficients decrease rapidly with diameter. This poses a numerical challenge due to the lack of a physical mechanism for diffusing numerical errors. For this reason, the minimum diffusion coefficient considered in the particle mass fraction transport equations corresponds to the fifth particle size node – any node greater than the fifth node is assigned the particle diffusion coefficient of the fifth node. • The mass flux of DPB from the heated rectangle is spatially uniform and all surfaces have spatially uniform temperature. • Particles t

hat impact a solid surface “stick” with 100% efficiency, and are removed from the flow. • The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly) in regions of the flow with recirculation, particularly behind the hot vapor source. The recirculation is characterized by high temperatures, long particle residency times, and the continuous introduction of additional vapor. The hydrodynamic and thermal fields, conversely, become steady after only a few seconds. Although a rigorous steady-state does not exist, all aerosol features develop and effectively stabilize shortly after the hydrodynamic fields. We therefore present all results at time t = 7 seconds, which is considered to be the effective steady-state. At his time, all fields are either steady, or changing at a rate that does not affect the conclusions drawn from the simulations.

When thermophoresis is active, as in panel (a), particles do not appear adjacent to the surface of the heated vapor source; the temperature gradient is large normal to the surface, and thermophoresis forces the particles out of this region. Small particles are able to diffuse out of the wake, resulting in lower particle number densities inside the Case 1MG-NT wake than the Case 1MG wake. Downstream of the wake, larger particle number densities are present in Case 1MG-NT relative to Case 1MG, following from the decreased number of particles trap

ped in the Case 1MG-NT wake vorticies. Figure 11 shows particle size distributions for Cases 1MG and 1MG-NT at time t = 7 seconds. Consistent with Fig. 10, the peak number density in Case 1MG-NT is greater than Case 1MG by approximately a factor of five – the most frequent particle size is ∼ 5 µm for both cases. A local maximum appears in both distributions around dp = 30 µm. This local maximum contains fewer particles in Case 1MG-NT than in Case 1MG, potentially because this local maximum is comprised of particles that have interacted with the wake region. In Case 1MG-NT, some of these particles have undergone evaporation and shifted to smaller particle sizes.

4.9 EFFECT OF HEATED VAPOR SOURCE ORIENTATION Figure 12 shows the particle number densities at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG-R in panel (a) and Case 1EG-R in panel (b) (where R stands for “Rotated”). Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R are identical to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦ . The wake regions of Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R are considerably smaller than Cases 1MG and 1EG, and neither Case 1MG-R nor Case 1EG-R contain particles in their wakes. The results from Case 1MG-R differ from Case 1MG in that they do not prominently display two high particle number density streaks around the symmetry line, but instead contain large particle number densities everywhere near the symmetry plane. Case 1EG-R presents large particle number densities near the cool upper surface, similar to Case 1EG. Unlike Case 1EG, Case 1EG-R does not contain particles inside its comparative

ly small downstream wake region, but instead contains particles in a large recirculation region that appears above the heated vapor source. The number density of particles in the recirculation region directly above the heated vapor source is lower than the particle number density downstream of the recirculation region. Settling

particles are not apparent, as in Case 1EG, which may be attributable to the lack of a wake region. Figure 13 shows particle size distributions for Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R at time t = 7 seconds. Both distributions present a single local maximum in particle size – the local maximum prominent at dp = 30 µm for Case 1MG is not present in Case 1MG-R. 4.10 EFFECT OF FLOW SPEED The Case 1 simulations were performed with an 8 cm/s inlet flow velocity. Case 2MG and Case 2EG consider a 10 cm/s inlet flow velocity. Particle number densities and velocity vectors for Case 2MG and Case 2EG are shown in Fig. 14 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a) shows Case 2MG and panel (b) shows Case 2EG. Case 2MG presents many features similar to Case 1MG, including symmetry about the center line and high particle number densities in the wake vortices. Case 2MG has an elongated wake associated with a higher flow speed. Case 2EG differs from Case 1EG in that particles are not prominent near the upper surface until much farther downstream – this is attributable to the decrease in Froude number, and corresponding decrease in upward motion due to buoyancy. Although the particle field remains asymmetric, the increased flow velocity has decreased the influence of bu

Particle size distributions for Case 2MG and Case 2EG computed at x0 = 26 and time t = 7 seconds are shown in Fig. 15. The most common particle size is ∼ 5 µm for both cases. 5 Summary We have simulated smoke formation and growth in microgravity and Earth gravity to examine how buoyancy and particle settling affect thermal/fluid/particle interactions and the resultant smoke particle size distributions. The simulated geometry emulates the SAME experiments performed aboard the International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015). Dibutyl pthalate (DBP) vapor is released from a heated rectangular sample, which serves as a surrogate for the smoldering material used in the SAME experiments. Large particles (> 30 µm) are present in the wake region downstream of the heated vapor source, and large particle number densities (∼ 1010 m−3 ) occur inside the wake vortices. The wake contains large particle number densities because dividing streamlines prevent the particles from being convected away, and the particles continue to grow as condensation consumes all available

DBP vapor. The particles simultaneously grow via coagulation. Downstream of the wake, two parallel particle streams contain high number densities of both large and small particles. No particles are present far downstream with diameter < 400 nm because nucleation only occurs for a short distance downstream of the heated vapor source. The particle size distributions contain local maximums near dp = 5 µm and dp = 35 µm for both flow speeds. The faster flow conditions present a slightly larger wake but this does not manifest as a meaningful difference in particle size distribution. Thermophoresis prevents particles from contacting the heated surface, which has been demonstrated by turning off the thermophoresis mechanism. Without thermophoresis, particles contact the heated vapor source and undergo evaporation. With respect to the particle size distribution, this has the effect of decreasin

g the number of large particles and increasing the number of small particles – this supports an assertion that the wake is responsible for producing the largest particles in the system. When gravity is present, all fields become asymmetric due to buoyant convection. Upward convection in the faster flow brings DBP vapor into close proximity with the cool upper surface, resulting in locally high nucleation rates near the upper wake vortex and the upper surface. Large particle number densities (∼ 1011 m−3 ) are present along the upper surface, and slightly lower number densities are present in the upper wake vortex. Comparably few particles are present in the lower wake vortex, where the diameter of average mass is maximized. Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling eliminates all particles with diameter > 35 µm. Unlike the microgravity case, the 8 cm/s Earth gravity case is

not bimodal, with a single local maximum at dp = 5 µm. Without particle settling, a bimodal distribution results with two local maximums at particle diameters comparable to the microgravity case. Rotating the heated vapor source 90◦ dramatically reduces the wake volume, and no particles appear in the small wake. Rotating the heated vapor source does not affect the Earth gravity case as significantly as the microgravity case. Increasing the flow speed from decreases the prominence of buoyancy, delays interaction with the upper surface until further downstream, widens the particle size distribution to include particles on the nanometer scale, and introduces a second local maximum to the PSD near dp = 30 µm. Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35 µm, wh

ile the terrestrial PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range. Alternatively, the microgravity PSD can be unimodal with a mode diameter of dp = 10 µm – roughly twice that of the terrestrial case. Results exhibit three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different recirculation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modifies aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion. Each of these factors tend to increase the size of par

ticles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. However, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar. In

contrast, a quiescent, enclosed system is a relevant case where Earth gravity and microgravity smoke are hypothesized to differ significantly, and is a consideration of future work. The Lab is Open Flying 250 miles above the Earth, the International Space Station (ISS) provides a platform for research to improve life on Earth, enable space exploration, and understand the universe. This Researcher’s Guide is intended to help potential ISS combustion science researchers plan experiments utilizing the microgravity environment in order to understand how heat and mass transport phenomena coupled with chemistry affect combustion behavior and fire safety. It covers the nature of the acceleration environment on ISS, available facilities for conducting combustion research, examples of previous microgravity investigations, and current combustion science and fire safety projects being developed for execution on the ISS.

Unique Features of the ISS Research Environment 1. M  icrogravity, or weightlessness, alters many observable phenomena within the physical and life sciences. Systems and processes affected by microgravity include surface wetting and interfacial tension, multiphase flow and heat transfer, multiphase system dynamics, solidification, and fire phenomena and combustion. Microgravity induces a vast array of changes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans, including global alterations in gene expression and 3-D aggregation of cells into tissue-like architecture.

2. E  xtreme conditions in the ISS environment include exposure to extreme heat and cold cycling, ultra-vacuum, atomic oxygen, and high-energy radiation. Testing and qualification of materials exposed to these extreme conditions have provided data to enable the manufacturing of long-life, reliable components used on Earth as well as in the world’s most sophisticated satellite and spacecraft components. 3. L  ow-Earth orbit at 51 degrees inclination and at a 90-minute orbit affords ISS a unique vantage point with an altitude of approximately 240 miles (400 kilometers) and an orbital path over 90 percent of the Earth’s population. This can provide improved spatial resolution and variable lighting conditions compared to the sun-synchronous orbits of typical Earth remote-sensing satellites.
